The same deity is listed in variant account 6 of section 8 under names such as 国作大己貴命 (reading unconfirmed) as other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (大国主神), and a story is told of his joining forces with Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto (少彦名命) to make the land.

nenokuni.title: The Persecution by the Eighty Deities and the Land 根の堅州国 (reading unconfirmed)
nenokuni.lead: 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed), chosen by Yakami-hime, is killed twice by his brothers, the Eighty Deities (八十神), and comes back to life, and he flees to 根堅州國 (reading unconfirmed), where Susanoo-no-Mikoto is. There, with the help of Suseri-bime, he gets through the ordeals set by Susanoo-no-Mikoto, is told "Become Ōkuninushi-no-Kami (大國主神)", returns to the earth, and begins making the land.

points.text: As 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) fled from 根堅州國 (reading unconfirmed), Susanoo-no-Mikoto called out to him from 黄泉比良坂 (reading unconfirmed): "Drive away your brothers with the living sword (生大刀) and the living bow and arrows (生弓矢), become Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and 宇都志國主神 (reading unconfirmed), make Suseri-bime (須世理毗賣) your principal wife, build a palace at the foot of 宇迦能山 (reading unconfirmed), and live there." With that sword and bow 大穴牟遲神 drove away the Eighty Deities and for the first time made the land.

Susanoo-no-Mikoto set 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) one ordeal after another: the chamber of snakes, the chamber of centipedes and bees, the field set on fire, and the picking of centipedes from his head. With the help of Suseri-bime's scarves (比礼), the tree nuts and red earth, and a mouse, 大穴牟遲神 got through them all.

The Eighty Deities (八十神) killed 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) twice, with a heated great rock and with a great tree into whose split a wedge had been driven. The first time, Kisakai-hime and Umukai-hime, sent by Kamumusuhi-no-Kami (神産巢日之命), brought 大穴牟遲神 back to life; the second time, 御祖命 (reading unconfirmed; his parent) did so.

大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) carried Suseri-bime on his back away from Susanoo-no-Mikoto's dwelling and fled, taking with him the living sword, the living bow and arrows, and the zither 天詔琴 (reading unconfirmed). The zither touched a tree and the earth rang and roared, so the great deity woke, but because his hair was tied to the rafters he could not catch up with them.

In the main text of section 8 of Book 1 of the Nihon Shoki, Ōanamuchi (大己貴神) is regarded as the child of Susanoo-no-Mikoto (素戔嗚尊) and 奇稻田姫 (reading unconfirmed), but in the Kojiki Ōkuninushi-no-Kami is a descendant of Susanoo-no-Mikoto in the sixth generation (K115), and in this story he becomes Susanoo-no-Mikoto's son-in-law. Passages corresponding to the persecution by the Eighty Deities and the ordeals in the land 根の国 (reading unconfirmed) could not be confirmed in Books 1 and 2 of the Nihon Shoki.

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, there are views that connect the two deaths and revivals and the ordeals in 根の堅州国 (reading unconfirmed) with coming-of-age rites, or that see them as a story of ordeals and growth leading to his becoming Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. The database also introduces a view that understands the change of his name from 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) to Ōkuninushi-no-Kami as a story of growth into a king.

story.text: The Eighty Deities (八十神) were angry and plotted to kill 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed). At the foot of the mountain 手間の山 in 伯岐國 (readings unconfirmed) they said, "We will drive a red boar down from the mountain, so wait below and catch it. If you do not catch it, we will kill you," and they heated in fire a great rock resembling a boar and rolled it down. 大穴牟遲神 caught it, was burned fast to the rock, and died. His parent, 御祖命 (reading unconfirmed), wept and grieved, went up to heaven and appealed to Kamumusuhi-no-Kami (神産巢日之命). Then Kisakai-hime and Umukai-hime were sent, and when Umukai-hime applied mother's milk, 大穴牟遲神 came back to life as a fine young man (麗壯夫) and went about once more.

Seeing this, the Eighty Deities again deceived 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) and led him into the mountains. They cut down a great tree, drove a wedge into it, had him go into the split, and then knocked out the wedge and crushed him to death. 御祖命 (reading unconfirmed) searched for him weeping, and on finding him split the tree, took him out and brought him back to life, saying, "If you stay here, you will in the end be destroyed by the Eighty Deities," and hurriedly sent him away to Ōyabiko-no-Kami in 木國 (reading unconfirmed). When the Eighty Deities came in pursuit, fitted arrows to their bows and demanded that he be handed over, 大穴牟遲神 was let slip away through the fork of a tree and told, "Go to 根堅州國 (reading unconfirmed), where Susanoo-no-Mikoto (written 須佐能男命) is. That great deity will surely arrange things well for you."

When he went to Susanoo-no-Mikoto's place as he had been told, Susanoo-no-Mikoto's daughter Suseri-bime came out, and they exchanged glances and became husband and wife. Suseri-bime told her father, "A very splendid deity has come," and the great deity came out, looked, and said, "This is the one called 葦原色許男 (reading unconfirmed)." The great deity called him in and made him sleep in the chamber of snakes, but Suseri-bime gave him a snake scarf (比礼, a cloth) and taught him, "If the snakes try to bite you, wave this three times and drive them off," so the snakes grew quiet, and he slept safely and came out. The next night he was put in the chamber of centipedes and bees, but in the same way he was given a scarf and came out safely.

Next the great deity shot a whistling arrow (鳴鏑, an arrow that makes a sound) into a wide field and had him fetch the arrow. When 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) went into the field, the great deity set fire to it all around and burned the field. While he could not find a way to escape, a mouse came and said, "Inside is 富良富良, outside is 須夫須夫," so he stamped on the spot, fell into a hole and was able to hide, and meanwhile the fire burned past. The mouse brought the whistling arrow in its mouth, but the arrow's feathers had been eaten by the mouse's young. Suseri-bime came weeping, carrying funeral implements, and the great deity too, thinking him dead, went out and stood in the field, but 大穴牟遲神 held out the arrow to him.

The great deity took 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) back to his house, called him into a wide great chamber, and had him pick the lice from his head. When he looked, there were many centipedes on the head. His wife gave him nuts of the 牟久 (reading unconfirmed) tree and red earth, and when he chewed up the nuts, held the red earth in his mouth and spat it out, the great deity thought he was chewing up the centipedes and spitting them out, felt fondness for him in his heart, and fell asleep. Then 大穴牟遲神 tied the great deity's hair to each of the rafters of the chamber, blocked the door with a great rock that would take five hundred men to pull, took Suseri-bime on his back, and fled carrying the great deity's living sword (生大刀), living bow and arrows (生弓矢) and the zither 天詔琴 (reading unconfirmed). At that moment the zither touched a tree and the earth rang and roared; the great deity woke in alarm and pulled down the chamber, but while he was untying his hair from the rafters, the two fled far away.

The great deity pursued them as far as 黄泉比良坂 (reading unconfirmed), gazed at them from afar, and called out to 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed): "With the living sword and the living bow and arrows that you carry, chase your half-brothers down to the foot of the slopes and drive them into the shallows of the rivers. Then you shall become Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and become 宇都志國主神 (reading unconfirmed), make my daughter Suseri-bime (須世理毗賣) your principal wife, raise thick palace pillars at the foot of 宇迦能山 (reading unconfirmed), make the crossed roof beams (千木) soar high enough to reach the High Plain of Heaven (高天原), and live there. You rascal!" With that sword and bow 大穴牟遲神 drove away the Eighty Deities, chasing them down at every slope and every river shallow, and for the first time made the land.

Yakami-hime, as she had promised before, was united with 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) and was brought to him, but, in awe of his principal wife Suseri-bime (須世理毗賣), she placed the child she had borne in the fork of a tree and went back home. Therefore that child was named Kimata-no-Kami, also called Mii-no-Kami. After this the story continues with 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed; another name of 大穴牟遲神) setting out to seek the hand of Nunakawa-hime of 高志國 (reading unconfirmed), and the scene in which he sings songs at her house.

quotes.note: The words: Go to 根堅州國 (reading unconfirmed), where Susanoo-no-Mikoto (written 須佐能男命) is. That great deity will surely arrange things well for you.
The words the mouse taught 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) in the burning field. A note in the original says that 富良富良 and 須夫須夫 are to be read by the sounds of the characters.
Susanoo-no-Mikoto's call: "You shall become Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, and also become 宇都志國主神 (reading unconfirmed)."
Chasing them down at the foot of every slope and driving them away at every river shallow, he for the first time made the land.

figures.name: 八十神 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The brothers of 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed), the Eighty Deities. Angry at not having been chosen by Yakami-hime, they kill 大穴牟遲神 twice, and then chase him as far as 木國 (reading unconfirmed).

figures.name: Kamumusuhi-no-Kami (神産巢日之命)
figures.role: At the appeal of 御祖命 (reading unconfirmed), sends Kisakai-hime and Umukai-hime and brings 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) back to life.

figures.name: Kisakai-hime (𧏛貝比賣)
figures.role: Sent by Kamumusuhi-no-Kami, she brings 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed), who had been burned to death, back to life together with Umukai-hime.

figures.name: Umukai-hime (蛤貝比賣)
figures.role: Applying mother's milk, she revives 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) as a fine young man.

figures.name: Ōyabiko-no-Kami (大屋毗古神)
figures.role: Shelters 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) in 木國 (reading unconfirmed), and when the Eighty Deities pursue him, lets him escape through the fork of a tree.

figures.name: Suseri-bime (須勢理毗賣; also written 須世理毗賣)
figures.role: The daughter of Susanoo-no-Mikoto. She is united with 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed), helps him through the ordeals by giving him scarves (比礼) and the tree nuts and red earth, and becomes his principal wife.

figures.name: Mouse (鼠)
figures.role: Shows 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed), surrounded by fire, a hole to hide in, and brings the whistling arrow in its mouth.

figures.name: 生大刀 and 生弓矢 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: The living sword and the living bow and arrows that 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) took from Susanoo-no-Mikoto's dwelling. With them he drives away the Eighty Deities.

figures.name: 天詔琴 (天沼琴) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The zither that 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed) took away. It touches a tree, makes the earth ring and roar, and wakes Susanoo-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: Yakami-hime (八上比賣)
figures.role: She is united with 大穴牟遲神 (reading unconfirmed), but, in awe of his principal wife Suseri-bime (須世理毗賣), she places the child she bore in the fork of a tree and goes back home.

figures.name: Kimata-no-Kami (木俣神), also Mii-no-Kami (御井神)
figures.role: The child Yakami-hime bore and left behind, placed in the fork of a tree.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, main text
compare.text: The main text says that Susanoo-no-Mikoto (素戔嗚尊) and 奇稻田姫 (reading unconfirmed) united and Ōanamuchi (大己貴神) was born, after which Susanoo-no-Mikoto went to 根國 (reading unconfirmed). It does not have the plot of the Kojiki, in which Ōkuninushi-no-Kami is a descendant of Susanoo-no-Mikoto and becomes his son-in-law in the land 根の国 (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, variant account 2
compare.text: Variant account 2 gives Ōanamuchi (大己貴命) as the grandson in the sixth generation of the child born of 奇稻田媛 (reading unconfirmed). In making him a descendant many generations after Susanoo-no-Mikoto, it is close to the genealogy of the Kojiki (K115).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, variant account 6
compare.text: Variant account 6 lists 葦原醜男, 八千戈神 and 顯國玉神 (readings unconfirmed), among others, as other names of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, but passages corresponding to the persecution by the Eighty Deities and the ordeals in the land 根の国 (reading unconfirmed) could not be confirmed in the main text or the variant accounts of Books 1 and 2.

kunitsukuri.title: The Songs of 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed) and Ōkuninushi-no-Kami's Making of the Land
kunitsukuri.lead: 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed; Ōkuninushi-no-Kami) seeks the hand of Nunakawa-hime of 高志國 (reading unconfirmed) with a song, and is reconciled with his jealous principal wife Suseri-bime by exchanging songs with her as well. After that, Ōkuninushi-no-Kami makes and firms up the land together with Sukunahikona-no-Kami (少名毗古那神), a child of Kamumusuhi-no-Kami, and after Sukunahikona-no-Kami leaves, he carries the making of the land forward by worshipping on 御諸山 (reading unconfirmed) a deity who came lighting up the sea.

points.text: Sukunahikona-no-Kami (少名毗古那神), who came from the sea riding in the boat 天之羅摩船 (reading unconfirmed), was revealed by Kuebiko to be a child of Kamumusuhi-no-Kami, and, at Kamumusuhi-no-Kami's command, made and firmed up the land side by side with 大穴牟遲 (reading unconfirmed; Ōkuninushi-no-Kami). Later Sukunahikona-no-Kami crossed over to 常世國 (reading unconfirmed).

After Sukunahikona-no-Kami left, a deity who approached lighting up the sea said, "If you worship me, I will make the land with you," and asked to be worshipped on the mountain to the east of the green fence of mountains (青垣) of Yamato (倭). The Kojiki records this as "the deity who dwells on 御諸山 (reading unconfirmed)" and does not write its name here.

八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed) sought the hand of Nunakawa-hime of 高志國 (reading unconfirmed) with a song; Nunakawa-hime too returned a song from inside the door, and they were united the following night. When his principal wife Suseri-bime (須勢理毗賣命) was jealous, 八千矛神 sang as he was about to set off for Yamato (倭); the consort offered a wine cup and sang in reply, and the two have remained settled together to this day. The Kojiki calls these songs "divine tales" (神語).

As children of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami are recorded 阿遲鉏高日子根神 (reading unconfirmed; now 迦毛大御神, reading unconfirmed) and 高比賣命 (reading unconfirmed), born of 多紀理毗賣命 (reading unconfirmed), and Kotoshironushi-no-Kami, born of Kamuyatate-hime-no-Mikoto. In the genealogy of Ōtoshi-no-Kami that follows appear the deity of the kitchen hearth worshipped by the people, and Ōyamakui-no-Kami, who dwells at 日枝山 and 松尾 (readings unconfirmed).

In variant account 6 of section 8 of the Nihon Shoki, Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto (少彥名命) is said to have come riding in a boat of 白蘞 bark and wearing the feathers of a wren (鷦鷯), and his parent is 高皇產靈尊 (reading unconfirmed). The deity who came lighting up the sea names itself the "幸魂奇魂" of Ōanamuchi (大己貴神) and is regarded as the deity of 大三輪 (reading unconfirmed) who dwells on 三諸山 (reading unconfirmed). In the Kojiki the parent is Kamumusuhi-no-Kami, and the deity of 御諸山 is written of as a deity separate from Ōkuninushi-no-Kami.

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, although the Kojiki calls him Ōkuninushi-no-Kami in this section, only in the one sentence about making and firming up the land with Sukunahikona-no-Kami does it use the name "大穴牟遲" (reading unconfirmed). This is thought to be because there was originally a myth pairing 大穴牟遲 and Sukunahikona, which was gathered together under the name of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami.

story.text: When 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed) arrived at the house of Nunakawa-hime of 高志國 (reading unconfirmed), he sang a song. The song tells how, having heard that there was a wise and beautiful maiden in the distant land of 高志, he came courting her, and how, as he kept standing in front of the board door of the house where the maiden slept, the nue birds and the pheasants, and the fowl in the yard, began to cry. Nunakawa-hime, without opening the door, returned a song from inside, answering that when night came she would come out. They did not meet that night, and on the night of the following day the two were united.

His principal consort (適后) Suseri-bime (須勢理毗賣命) was intensely jealous. The husband deity prepared for a journey to go up from Izumo to the land of Yamato (倭國), and with one hand on the saddle of his horse and one foot in the stirrup, he sang. In the song he calls to his wife: trying on black robes and blue robes, he throws them off as unbecoming, puts on a dyed robe and says this one is good; and if he goes away like a flock of birds, though she says she will not weep, she will weep.

The consort took a large wine cup in her hand, drew close to her husband, and sang as she offered it to him. In the song she sings that since he is a man he can have a wife on every island and every rocky shore wherever he goes, but that she, a woman, has no husband other than him, and invites him to rest together beneath the soft bedclothes and to drink the wine. Having sung thus, the two "宇伎由比" and "宇那賀氣理" (both words written by the sounds of the characters), and have remained settled together to this day. These songs are called "divine tales" (神語).

Ōkuninushi-no-Kami took as wife 多紀理毗賣命 (reading unconfirmed), who dwells at the 奧津宮 shrine of 胸形 (readings unconfirmed), and 阿遲鉏高日子根神 and his younger sister 高比賣命 (also called 下光比賣命) (readings unconfirmed) were born. 阿遲鉏高日子根神 is the deity now called 迦毛大御神 (reading unconfirmed). He also took Kamuyatate-hime-no-Mikoto as wife, and Kotoshironushi-no-Kami was born. The genealogy of descendants continues further, and the deities from Yashimajinumi-no-Kami to 遠津山岬帶神 (reading unconfirmed) are summed up as "the seventeen generations of deities" (十七世の神).

When Ōkuninushi-no-Kami was at the cape 御大の御前 (reading unconfirmed) in Izumo, a deity came along the crests of the waves riding in the boat 天之羅摩船 (reading unconfirmed), wearing as clothing the whole skin stripped from a goose (鵝). When asked its name it did not answer, and the deities attending him did not know either, but Taniguku said, "Kuebiko should know." Kuebiko answered, "This is Sukunahikona-no-Kami (少名毗古那神), the child of Kamumusuhi-no-Kami," and Kamumusuhi-no-Kami also declared, "He is truly my child, and among my children he is the one who slipped out between the fingers of my hand. Become brothers with you, 葦原色許男命 (reading unconfirmed), and make and firm up the land." So the two deities 大穴牟遲 (reading unconfirmed) and Sukunahikona made and firmed up the land side by side, but later Sukunahikona-no-Kami crossed over to 常世國 (reading unconfirmed). Kuebiko, who revealed Sukunahikona-no-Kami's name, is written to be what is now Yamada-no-Sohodo, a deity who cannot walk on its feet but knows everything under heaven.

Ōkuninushi-no-Kami lamented, "How could I make this land alone? With which deity could I make it together?" At that moment there was a deity who approached lighting up the sea and said, "If you worship me well, I will complete the making of the land with you. Otherwise the land will be hard to complete." When Ōkuninushi-no-Kami asked how he should worship it, the deity answered, "Worship me with reverence on the mountain to the east of the green fence of mountains (青垣) of Yamato (倭)." This is the deity who dwells on 御諸山 (reading unconfirmed).

Next the genealogy of the descendants of Ōtoshi-no-Kami is recorded. Ōtoshi-no-Kami took 伊怒比賣 as wife and fathered Ōkunimitama-no-Kami, 韓神, 曾富理神, 白日神 and 聖神; took 香用比賣 as wife and fathered 大香山戶臣神 and 年御神; and took 天知迦流美豆比賣 as wife and fathered 奧津日子神 (readings unconfirmed), Okutsu-hime-no-Mikoto (also called 大戶比賣神, reading unconfirmed) and others. Okutsu-hime-no-Mikoto (大戶比賣神) is recorded as "the deity of the kitchen hearth worshipped by the people", and Ōyamakui-no-Kami (also called 山末之大主神, reading unconfirmed) is written to dwell at 日枝山 in 近淡海國 and at 松尾 in 葛野 (readings unconfirmed), and to be a deity who uses a whistling arrow (鳴鏑). The children of Ōtoshi-no-Kami number sixteen deities in all, and further, Hayamato-no-Kami took 大氣都比賣神 (reading unconfirmed) as wife, and eight deities, including 若山咋神 and 若年神 (readings unconfirmed), were born.

quotes.note: Sukunahikona-no-Kami came from the crests of the waves riding in the boat 天之羅摩船 (reading unconfirmed), wearing as clothing the whole skin stripped from a goose.
The two deities 大穴牟遲 (reading unconfirmed) and Sukunahikona, side by side, made and firmed up this land.
The words of the deity who came lighting up the sea: "Worship me with reverence on the mountain to the east of the green fence of mountains of Yamato."
The text concludes that the exchange of songs among 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed), Nunakawa-hime and Suseri-bime is called "divine tales" (神語).

figures.name: Nunakawa-hime (沼河比賣; also written 沼河日賣)
figures.role: A goddess of 高志國 (reading unconfirmed). She answers the courtship song of 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed) with a song from inside the door, and they are united the following night.

figures.name: Suseri-bime (須勢理毗賣命)
figures.role: The principal wife (適后) of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami. She is jealous of his courtship of Nunakawa-hime, but offers a wine cup, sings, and is reconciled with her husband.

figures.name: 天之羅摩船 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The boat in which Sukunahikona-no-Kami came riding along the crests of the waves.

figures.name: Taniguku (多迩具久)
figures.role: About Sukunahikona-no-Kami, whose name nobody knew, it offers that "Kuebiko would know."

figures.name: Kuebiko (久延毗古), also Yamada-no-Sohodo (山田之曾富騰)
figures.role: Reveals the identity of Sukunahikona-no-Kami. It is regarded as a deity who cannot walk on its feet but knows everything under heaven.

figures.name: Kamumusuhi-no-Kami (神産巢日神; also 神産巢日御祖命)
figures.role: Acknowledges Sukunahikona-no-Kami as its child, and commands him to become brothers with Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and make and firm up the land.

figures.name: Kamuyatate-hime-no-Mikoto (神屋楯比賣命)
figures.role: A wife of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and the mother of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami.

figures.name: Ōkunimitama-no-Kami (大國御魂神)
figures.role: One of the children Ōtoshi-no-Kami fathered after taking 伊怒比賣 (reading unconfirmed) as wife.

figures.name: Okutsu-hime-no-Mikoto (奧津比賣命; also 大戶比賣神)
figures.role: A child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami. She is recorded as the deity of the kitchen hearth worshipped by the people.

figures.name: Hayamato-no-Kami (羽山戶神)
figures.role: A child of Ōtoshi-no-Kami. He takes 大氣都比賣神 (reading unconfirmed) as wife and becomes the father of eight deities, including 若山咋神 (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, variant account 6
compare.text: Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto (少彥名命) is said to have come riding on the tide with 白蘞 bark as his boat and the feathers of a wren (鷦鷯) as his clothing, and his parent is 高皇產靈尊 (reading unconfirmed). In the Kojiki it is the boat 天之羅摩船 (reading unconfirmed) and the skin of a goose (鵝), and the parent is Kamumusuhi-no-Kami.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, variant account 6
compare.text: The deity who came lighting up the sea names itself the "幸魂奇魂" of Ōanamuchi (大己貴神), and is regarded as the deity of 大三輪 (reading unconfirmed) who dwells on 三諸山 (reading unconfirmed). In the Kojiki this deity does not give its name, and is written of as "the deity who dwells on 御諸山" (reading unconfirmed), separate from Ōkuninushi-no-Kami.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 1, section 8, variant account 6
compare.text: It is said that Sukunahikona-no-Mikoto (少彥名命) went from the cape 御碕 (reading unconfirmed) of Kumano to 常世郷 (reading unconfirmed), and also that on Awashima (淡嶋) he climbed a stalk of millet, was flicked off, and crossed over to 常世郷. The Kojiki records only that he crossed over to 常世國 (reading unconfirmed). Passages corresponding to the songs of 八千矛神 (reading unconfirmed) with Nunakawa-hime and Suseri-bime could not be confirmed.

amewakahiko.title: Ame-no-Wakahiko (天若日子)
amewakahiko.lead: Ame-no-Wakahiko (天若日子), sent from Takamanohara to bring the Central Land of the Reed Plains (葦原中国) into submission, married a daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and made no report for eight years. Because he shot the pheasant that came to question him, he died by that very arrow when 高木神 (reading unconfirmed) threw it back. Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami, who came to the funeral, was mistaken for the dead man, flew into a rage and cut down the mourning house.

points.text: As envoys to bring the Central Land of the Reed Plains into submission, Ame-no-Hohi-no-Kami (天菩比神) was sent first, but he fawned on Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and made no report for three years. Ame-no-Wakahiko, who was sent next, also married Shitateru-hime (下照比売), tried to make the land his own, and made no report for eight years.

On the advice of Ame-no-Sagume (天佐具売), Ame-no-Wakahiko shot dead the pheasant Nakime (鳴女), who had come to ask him why. 高木神 (reading unconfirmed) threw that arrow back, saying “If he has an evil heart, let it strike him,” and the arrow struck Ame-no-Wakahiko in the chest as he lay asleep, and he died. The Kojiki presents this as the origin of the “returning arrow” (還矢) and of the “pheasant's one-way errand” (雉之頓使).

Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami, who came to the funeral, looked exactly like Ame-no-Wakahiko and was mistaken for the dead man. In his anger he cut down the mourning house with his ten-fist sword (十掬剣) and kicked it away. The Kojiki explains that this became 喪山 (the Mourning Mountain; reading unconfirmed) at the upper reaches of the 藍見河 (reading unconfirmed) in the land of Mino.
To make known the name of Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami as he flew away, his younger sister 高比売命 (reading unconfirmed) composed a song, and the Kojiki calls this song a 夷振 (reading unconfirmed) song.

In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, section 9, Ame-no-Wakahiko's father 天国玉 (reading unconfirmed) sends a gale to carry the body up to heaven, and he is mourned in a mourning house built in heaven. In the Kojiki, his father, wife and children come down to the earth and build the mourning house on the spot.

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, because the story of Ame-no-Wakahiko strays from the main thread of the ceding of the land, it is thought to have originally been transmitted separately from the land-ceding story. Views on the reading of his name are also divided, with readings such as Amewakahiko and Ame-no-Wakahiko.

story.text: Amaterasu-Ōmikami declared that the Land of Abundant Reed Plains and Fresh Rice Ears (豊葦原水穂国) was a land to be ruled by her child Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto, and she sought to send him down from heaven. But Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto looked down from the Floating Bridge of Heaven (天浮橋), said “伊多久佐夜藝弖有那理” (it seems to be in great uproar), turned back and reported this to Amaterasu-Ōmikami. Takamimusubi-no-Kami and Amaterasu-Ōmikami then gathered the eight hundred myriad deities on the riverbed of the Heavenly River Yasu (天安河) and had Omoikane-no-Kami (思金神) think the matter over. Since there were many violent earthly deities on the earth, they discussed which deity to send to subdue them, and decided to send Ame-no-Hohi-no-Kami (天菩比神). However, Ame-no-Hohi-no-Kami fawned on Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and submitted to him, and even after three years he made no report.

Next, on the advice of Omoikane-no-Kami, they gave Ame-no-Wakahiko (天若日子), the son of Amatsukunitama-no-Kami (天津国玉神), the bow 天之麻迦古弓 and the arrows 天之波波矢 (readings unconfirmed), and sent him off. When Ame-no-Wakahiko came down to the earth, he married Shitateru-hime (下照比売), a daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, plotted to obtain the land for himself, and even after eight years he made no report. When Amaterasu-Ōmikami and Takamimusubi-no-Kami discussed whom to send to ask why, the deities recommended sending a pheasant named Nakime (鳴女).

Nakime perched on the sacred katsura tree (湯津楓) at the gate of Ame-no-Wakahiko's house and delivered the words of the heavenly deities exactly as given. Ame-no-Sagume (天佐具売), hearing this, urged him, “This bird's cry is very bad, so you should shoot it dead,” and Ame-no-Wakahiko shot the pheasant dead with the bow and arrows he had received from the heavenly deities. The arrow pierced the pheasant's breast, rose all the way to heaven, and reached Amaterasu-Ōmikami and 高木神 (reading unconfirmed; another name of Takamimusubi-no-Kami), who were on the riverbed of the Heavenly River Yasu. 高木神 saw that the bloodied arrow was the one given to Ame-no-Wakahiko, and threw it back, saying, “If he has kept his orders and shot at evil deities, let it not strike him. If he has an evil heart, let it strike him.” The arrow struck Ame-no-Wakahiko in the chest as he lay in his bed in the morning, and he died. The Kojiki records that this was the origin of the “returning arrow” (還矢), and that because the pheasant did not return, the proverb “the pheasant's one-way errand” (雉之頓使) came into being.

The weeping of Shitateru-hime, who had lost her husband, reached all the way to heaven on the wind. Ame-no-Wakahiko's father Amatsukunitama-no-Kami, who was in heaven, and Ame-no-Wakahiko's wife and children heard it, came down, and built a mourning house on that spot. They assigned the duties of the funeral to the river goose, the heron, the kingfisher, the sparrow and the pheasant, and mourned him with eight days and eight nights of ritual music and dance.

Then Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami came to offer condolences. Because he looked exactly like Ame-no-Wakahiko, Ame-no-Wakahiko's father and wife clung to his hands and feet and wept, saying “My child was not dead!” and “My lord was not dead!” Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami was furious, saying, “I came to mourn only because he was a dear friend. Why do you compare me to an unclean dead man?” He cut down the mourning house with the ten-fist sword (十掬剣) at his waist and kicked it away with his feet. The Kojiki records that this is 喪山 (the Mourning Mountain; reading unconfirmed) at the upper reaches of the 藍見河 (reading unconfirmed) in the land of Mino, and that the sword was named 大量 (reading unconfirmed), also called 神度剣 (reading unconfirmed).

As Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami flew off in anger, his younger sister by the same mother, 高比売命 (reading unconfirmed), composed a song to make her brother's name known. At the end of the song her brother's name is woven in: “阿治志貴多迦比古泥能迦微曾也”. The Kojiki records that this song is a 夷振 (reading unconfirmed) song.

quotes.note: At once he married Shitateru-hime, the daughter of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, plotted to obtain the land, and even after eight years he made no report.
If Ame-no-Wakahiko has an evil heart, let him be struck by this arrow and die (the words of 高木神 (reading unconfirmed) as he throws the arrow back).
What is called in today's proverb “the pheasant's one-way errand” (an envoy who goes and never comes back) originates here.
I came only to mourn, because he was a dear friend. Why do you compare me to an unclean dead man? (the angry words of Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami).

figures.name: Ame-no-Hohi-no-Kami (天菩比神)
figures.role: Sent to the earth as the first envoy, but he fawned on Ōkuninushi-no-Kami and made no report for three years.

figures.name: Amatsukunitama-no-Kami (天津國玉神)
figures.role: Father of Ame-no-Wakahiko. Learning of his son's death, he came down from heaven, built a mourning house and mourned him.

figures.name: Nakime (鳴女)
figures.role: The pheasant sent to ask Ame-no-Wakahiko why he made no report. She was shot dead by Ame-no-Wakahiko.

figures.name: Ame-no-Sagume (天佐具賣)
figures.role: Said that Nakime's cry was bad and urged Ame-no-Wakahiko to shoot her dead.

figures.name: 天之麻迦古弓 and 天之波波矢 (readings unconfirmed)
figures.role: The bow and arrows given to Ame-no-Wakahiko when he set out as envoy. This arrow pierced the pheasant and reached heaven, and when thrown back it killed Ame-no-Wakahiko.

figures.name: Mourning house (喪屋)
figures.role: The building made for Ame-no-Wakahiko's funeral. It was cut down by Ajisukitakahikone-no-Kami and is regarded as having become 喪山 (the Mourning Mountain) in the land of Mino.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 9, because Ame-no-Hohi-no-Mikoto (天穂日命) made no report, his son 大背飯三熊之大人 (reading unconfirmed) was also sent, but he too followed his father and made no report. This deity does not appear in the Kojiki.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 9, Ame-no-Wakahiko's (天稚彦) father 天国玉 (reading unconfirmed) carries the body up to heaven with a gale, and there builds a mourning house and mourns him. In the Kojiki, the father, wife and children come down to the earth and build the mourning house.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, variant account 6
compare.text: In variant account 6 of section 9, the male pheasant sent first sees fields of millet and beans, alights there and does not return, and this is given as the origin of the expression “雉頓” (the pheasant's one-way errand). In the Kojiki, the expression “the pheasant's one-way errand” arises from the fact that Nakime, shot dead by Ame-no-Wakahiko, did not return.

kuniyuzuri.title: The Ceding of the Land
kuniyuzuri.lead: Takemikazuchi-no-Kami (建御雷神), sent from Takamanohara, pressed Ōkuninushi-no-Kami on the beach of 伊耶佐 (reading unconfirmed) in Izumo to cede the land. His son Kotoshironushi-no-Kami consented, and Takeminakata-no-Kami, who challenged Takemikazuchi to a trial of strength, was chased as far as the sea of Suwa (州羽海) in Shinano (科野) and surrendered. Ōkuninushi-no-Kami offered up the Central Land of the Reed Plains on condition that a magnificent dwelling be built for him, and Takemikazuchi-no-Kami reported that the land had been pacified.

points.text: As envoy for the ceding of the land, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, son of 伊都之尾羽張神 (reading unconfirmed), was sent with Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami as his companion. The two deities stood a ten-fist sword (十掬剣) upside down on the crest of a wave on the small beach of 伊耶佐 (reading unconfirmed) in Izumo, sat on its point, and demanded that Ōkuninushi-no-Kami cede the land.

Ōkuninushi-no-Kami left the answer to his son. Kotoshironushi-no-Kami consented, saying “I will give this land to the child of the heavenly deities,” then trod on his boat to tip it over, clapped his hands in the reverse “heavenly” manner (天逆手), and hid inside a fence of green brushwood (青柴垣).

Takeminakata-no-Kami challenged Takemikazuchi to a trial of strength, but Takemikazuchi-no-Kami's hand turned into an icicle and then into a sword blade, and he was no match. Driven as far as the sea of Suwa (州羽海) in the land of Shinano (科野国), he swore “I will not leave this place” and agreed to give up the land.

Ōkuninushi-no-Kami offered up the Central Land of the Reed Plains on condition that a dwelling be built for him with thick pillars and high crossed roof-beams (氷木), like the palace of the child of the heavenly deities, and said that he himself would withdraw into hiding and serve. Thus Takemikazuchi-no-Kami reported that the land had been pacified.

In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, section 9, the deities sent are the two deities Futsunushi-no-Kami (経津主神) and Takemikazuchi-no-Kami (武甕槌神), and no deity corresponding to Takeminakata-no-Kami appears. Ōanamuchi-no-Kami (大己貴神; that is, Ōkuninushi-no-Kami) gives the two deities the broad spear he used when he pacified the land, and withdraws into hiding.

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, in the scene at the small beach of 多芸志 (reading unconfirmed), the text does not make clear who built the heavenly dwelling (天之御舎) or who presented a feast to whom, so interpretations are divided: one view holds that the heavenly side entertained Ōkuninushi-no-Kami, another that Ōkuninushi-no-Kami made the offering to the heavenly deities, and so on.

story.text: After the failure of Ame-no-Wakahiko, Amaterasu-Ōmikami again asked whom to send, and Omoikane-no-Kami and the other deities recommended 伊都之尾羽張神 (reading unconfirmed), who dwelt in the Heavenly Rock Dwelling (天石屋) at the upper reaches of the Heavenly River Yasu (天安河), or his son Takemikazuchi-no-O-no-Kami (建御雷之男神). Because 伊都之尾羽張神 had dammed the waters of the Heavenly River Yasu and blocked the way, no other deity could go there, so Ame-no-Kaku-no-Kami (天迦久神) was sent as messenger. 伊都之尾羽張神 accepted the request and offered up his son Takemikazuchi-no-Kami. Thus Takemikazuchi-no-Kami was sent, with Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami accompanying him.

The two deities descended to the small beach of 伊耶佐 (reading unconfirmed) in the land of Izumo, drew a ten-fist sword (十掬剣), thrust it upside down into the crest of a wave, and sat cross-legged on the point of the sword. Then they asked Ōkuninushi-no-Kami: “We ask by command of Amaterasu-Ōmikami and 高木神 (reading unconfirmed). The Central Land of the Reed Plains that you rule has been entrusted to our child as a land for him to rule. What is your mind?” Ōkuninushi-no-Kami answered that he could not answer himself; his son Yae-kotoshironushi-no-Kami (八重言代主神) should answer, but he had gone out to the cape of 御大 (reading unconfirmed) to catch birds and fish and had not yet returned.

When Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami summoned Kotoshironushi-no-Kami and questioned him, Kotoshironushi-no-Kami said to his father, “It is an awesome command. I will give this land to the child of the heavenly deities.” Then he trod on the boat he had come in to tip it over, clapped his hands in the reverse “heavenly” manner (天逆手), turned the boat into a fence of green brushwood (青柴垣), and hid inside it.

Asked whether he had any other son who should answer, Ōkuninushi-no-Kami named Takeminakata-no-Kami. Just then Takeminakata-no-Kami arrived, holding up on his fingertips a great rock that would take a thousand men to pull, challenged Takemikazuchi to a trial of strength, and seized Takemikazuchi-no-Kami's hand. At once Takemikazuchi-no-Kami's hand turned into an icicle and then into a sword blade, so Takeminakata-no-Kami drew back in fear. Next Takemikazuchi-no-Kami seized Takeminakata-no-Kami's hand like a young reed, crushed it, and flung him away, and Takeminakata-no-Kami fled. Takemikazuchi-no-Kami pursued him as far as the sea of Suwa (州羽海) in the land of Shinano (科野国), and when he was about to kill him, Takeminakata-no-Kami begged: “Do not kill me. I will not go out of this place, nor will I go against the words of my father or of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami. I will give up the Central Land of the Reed Plains as the child of the heavenly deities commands.”

When Takemikazuchi-no-Kami returned and asked again, Ōkuninushi-no-Kami answered that it was as his two sons had said, that he too would not go against it, and that he would give up the Central Land of the Reed Plains. However, he stated that if his dwelling place were built like the palace where the child of the heavenly deities lives, with thick pillars set firmly on the bedrock deep in the earth and crossed roof-beams (氷木) soaring high enough to reach Takamanohara, he would withdraw into a far corner and serve. He also said that if Yae-kotoshironushi-no-Kami (八重事代主神) took the lead in serving, none of his many deity children would rebel.

A heavenly dwelling (天之御舎) was built at the small beach of 多芸志 (reading unconfirmed) in the land of Izumo, and Kushiyatama-no-Kami (櫛八玉神), grandson of 水戸神 (reading unconfirmed), served as cook and presented a heavenly feast. Kushiyatama-no-Kami became a cormorant, dived to the bottom of the sea, brought up clay in his beak, made many flat vessels, made a fire-drill from the stems of seaweed, and kindled fire. Then words of blessing were spoken: that this fire would blaze in Takamanohara until the soot hung long in the new palace of Kamumusubi (神産巣日御祖命), would bake hard the earth below down to the bedrock, and that a great sea bass caught by the fishermen would be cooked and presented. After that, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami returned to Takamanohara and reported that he had pacified the Central Land of the Reed Plains.

quotes.note: They drew a ten-fist sword, thrust it upside down into the crest of a wave, and sat cross-legged on the point of the sword.
It is an awesome command. I will give this land to the child of the heavenly deities (the words of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami).
(When Takeminakata-no-Kami seized his hand) Takemikazuchi-no-Kami's hand at once became an icicle, and then a sword blade.
I will withdraw into a far, winding corner and serve (the words of Ōkuninushi-no-Kami).

figures.name: 伊都之尾羽張神 (reading unconfirmed), also called Ame-no-Ohabari-no-Kami (天尾羽張神)
figures.role: Father of Takemikazuchi-no-Kami, dwelling in the Heavenly Rock Dwelling at the upper reaches of the Heavenly River Yasu. Asked to serve as envoy, he offered his son Takemikazuchi-no-Kami in his place.

figures.name: Ame-no-Kaku-no-Kami (天迦久神)
figures.role: Sent to ask the intentions of 伊都之尾羽張神 (reading unconfirmed), who was blocking the way.

figures.name: Kushiyatama-no-Kami (櫛八玉神)
figures.role: Grandson of 水戸神 (reading unconfirmed). At the small beach of 多芸志 (reading unconfirmed) he served as cook; becoming a cormorant, he made vessels from clay from the sea floor, kindled fire and presented a feast.

figures.name: Ten-fist sword (十掬釼)
figures.role: The sword that Takemikazuchi-no-Kami thrust upside down into the crest of a wave and sat upon its point.

figures.name: Fence of green brushwood (青柴垣)
figures.role: The fence into which Kotoshironushi-no-Kami turned his boat by clapping his hands in the reverse “heavenly” manner. Kotoshironushi-no-Kami hid inside it.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 9, Futsunushi-no-Kami (経津主神) is chosen first, Takemikazuchi-no-Kami (武甕槌神) steps forward to join him, and the two deities are sent together. In the Kojiki, Ame-no-Torifune-no-Kami accompanies Takemikazuchi-no-Kami (建御雷神), and Futsunushi-no-Kami does not appear.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 9, there is no trial of strength with Takeminakata-no-Kami; Ōanamuchi-no-Kami (大己貴神), accepting the words of Kotoshironushi-no-Kami, gives the two deities the broad spear he used when he pacified the land, and withdraws into hiding.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, variant account 2
compare.text: In variant account 2 of section 9, Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto (高皇産霊尊) commands that the affairs of the visible world be governed by the imperial grandson and that Ōanamuchi-no-Kami govern divine affairs, and promises to build the 天日隅宮 (reading unconfirmed) for him.

tenson.title: The Descent of the Heavenly Grandson
tenson.lead: Once the Central Land of the Reed Plains had been pacified, Ninigi-no-Mikoto, son of Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto, went down in his father's place. Guided by Sarutahiko-no-Kami and accompanied by the deities of the five attendant groups (五伴緒), and having received the curved jewels, the mirror and the sword, he descended to Takachiho in Hyūga in Tsukushi. Afterwards Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto escorted Sarutahiko-no-Kami home, took on his name, and became the origin of the Sarume no Kimi (猿女君).

points.text: Amaterasu-Ōmikami and 高木神 (reading unconfirmed) at first commanded Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto to go down, but while he was making ready his son Ninigi-no-Mikoto was born, so at Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto's request it was decided that Ninigi-no-Mikoto would go down in his place.

At the Eightfold Crossroads of Heaven (天八衢), there was a deity shining on both Takamanohara and the Central Land of the Reed Plains. When Ame-no-Uzume-no-Kami questioned him, he gave his name as Sarutahiko-no-Kami, an earthly deity, and answered that he had come to meet the Heavenly Grandson in order to guide him.

Ninigi-no-Mikoto was accompanied by the five attendant groups (五伴緒): Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, Futodama-no-Mikoto (布刀玉命), Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto (伊斯許理度売命) and Tamanooya-no-Mikoto. He received the eight-shaku curved jewels (八尺勾玉), the mirror and the Kusanagi sword (草那芸剣). Amaterasu-Ōmikami commanded that the mirror be worshipped as her own spirit, just as one would worship her.

Ninigi-no-Mikoto pushed through the clouds, passed by way of the Floating Bridge of Heaven, and descended to 久士布流多気 (reading unconfirmed) at Takachiho in Hyūga in Tsukushi. Ame-no-Oshihi-no-Mikoto and Amatsukume-no-Mikoto led the way in arms, and Ninigi-no-Mikoto praised this land as a good land “where the morning sun shines straight and the evening sun shines bright,” and built his palace there.

Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto escorted Sarutahiko-no-Kami home and took on his name, becoming the origin of the Sarume no Kimi. Also, because she slit with a small knife the mouth of the sea cucumber, which alone did not answer that it would serve the Heavenly Grandson, the Kojiki records that the sea cucumber's mouth is split to this day.

In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, section 9, Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto (高皇産霊尊) covers the imperial grandson with a bed-covering (真床追衾) and sends him down; neither the story of the bestowal of the curved jewels, mirror and sword nor Sarutahiko appears. The three treasures, the deities of the five groups (五部神) and Sarutahiko's coming to meet him appear in variant account 1.

story.text: Having received the report of pacification, Amaterasu-Ōmikami and 高木神 (reading unconfirmed) commanded the crown prince Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto to go down to the earth and rule it. Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto answered, “While I was making ready to go down, a child was born. This child should be sent down.” This child was the younger of the two born to Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto and Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime-no-Mikoto (万幡豊秋津師比売命), daughter of 高木神; the elder was Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto (天火明命). Thus the command to rule the Land of Abundant Reed Plains and Fresh Rice Ears was given to 日子番能邇邇芸命 (Ninigi-no-Mikoto).

When Ninigi-no-Mikoto was about to come down from heaven, at the Eightfold Crossroads of Heaven (天八衢; a place where roads divide) there was a deity who shone above on Takamanohara and below on the Central Land of the Reed Plains. Amaterasu-Ōmikami and 高木神 (reading unconfirmed) commanded Ame-no-Uzume-no-Kami: “Though you are a delicate woman, you are a deity who wins a staring contest against any deity you face, so go and question him.” That deity answered, “I am an earthly deity, and my name is Sarutahiko-no-Kami. I heard that the child of the heavenly deities was coming down, so I have come to meet him, to serve as his guide.”

The five attendant groups (五伴緒), Ame-no-Koyane-no-Mikoto, Futodama-no-Mikoto (布刀玉命), Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, Ishikoridome-no-Mikoto (伊斯許理度売命) and Tamanooya-no-Mikoto, were assigned to Ninigi-no-Mikoto. In addition, the eight-shaku curved jewels (八尺勾玉), the mirror and the Kusanagi sword (草那芸剣) were added, along with Tokoyo-no-Omoikane-no-Kami (常世思金神), Tajikarao-no-Kami (手力男神) and Ame-no-Iwatowake-no-Kami (天石門別神). Amaterasu-Ōmikami commanded, “Worship this mirror as my spirit, just as you would worship me. Omoikane-no-Kami, take charge of the affairs of the worship and carry them out.” It is recorded that these two deities were worshipped at “佐久久斯侶，伊須受能宫”. Toyouke-no-Kami (登由宇気神) is regarded as the deity dwelling at 度相 (reading unconfirmed) of the Outer Shrine, Ame-no-Iwatowake-no-Kami (天石戸別神) as a deity of the gates, and Tajikarao-no-Kami as the deity dwelling at 佐那那県 (reading unconfirmed); the five attendant groups are regarded as the ancestors of the Nakatomi no Muraji (中臣連), the 忌部首 (reading unconfirmed), the Sarume no Kimi (猿女君), the 作鏡連 (reading unconfirmed) and the Tamanooya no Muraji (玉祖連), respectively.

Ninigi-no-Mikoto left the heavenly rock seat (天石位), pushed apart the many-layered clouds, passed by way of the Floating Bridge of Heaven, and descended to 久士布流多気 (reading unconfirmed) at Takachiho in Hyūga in Tsukushi. Ame-no-Oshihi-no-Mikoto and Amatsukume-no-Mikoto, carrying stone quivers on their backs, wearing mallet-headed swords (頭椎大刀) and holding bows and arrows, went at the front and served him. The two are regarded as the ancestors of the Ōtomo no Muraji (大伴連) and the Kume no Atai (久米直), respectively. Ninigi-no-Mikoto said that this land faces 韓国 (reading unconfirmed), leads straight to the cape of 笠紗 (reading unconfirmed), and is a land where the morning sun shines straight and the evening sun shines bright, and so it is a very good land; and he dwelt in a palace with thick pillars set on the bedrock deep in the earth and crossed roof-beams (氷椽) soaring high enough to reach Takamanohara.

Ninigi-no-Mikoto commanded Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto: “You who revealed the identity of Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami, who guided me, shall escort him home, take on that deity's name and serve.” It is said that this is why the Sarume no Kimi bear the name of the male deity Sarutahiko and their women are called Sarume no Kimi. While Sarutahiko-no-Kami was at 阿耶訶 (reading unconfirmed), he was fishing when his hand was caught by a 比良夫 shellfish (reading unconfirmed), and he sank into the sea and drowned. His name when he sank to the bottom is Sokodoku-mitama (底度久御魂), his name when the sea water rose in bubbles is Tsubutatsu-mitama (都夫多都御魂), and his name when the foam burst is Awasaku-mitama (阿和佐久御魂).

Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto, returning after escorting Sarutahiko-no-Kami, gathered all the fish, large and small, and asked, “Will you serve the child of the heavenly deities?” All the fish answered, “We will serve,” but only the sea cucumber did not answer. Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto said, “Is this a mouth that does not answer?” and slit the sea cucumber's mouth with a small knife, and so the sea cucumber's mouth is split to this day. For this reason, it is said, whenever the “swift offerings of the islands” (嶋之速贄) are presented, generation after generation, a share is also given to the Sarume no Kimi.

quotes.note: I am an earthly deity, and my name is Sarutahiko-no-Kami (his answer when questioned at the Eightfold Crossroads of Heaven).
(Worship) this mirror wholly as my spirit, just as you would worship me.
It is a land where the morning sun shines straight, a land where the evening sun shines bright (Ninigi-no-Mikoto's words praising the land to which he descended).
Is this a mouth that does not answer? (the words of Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto to the sea cucumber).

figures.name: Yorozuhata-toyoakitsushi-hime-no-Mikoto (萬幡豊秋津師比賣命)
figures.role: Daughter of 高木神 (reading unconfirmed). With Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto she bore Ame-no-Hoakari-no-Mikoto and Ninigi-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: Ame-no-Iwatowake-no-Kami (天石門別神)
figures.role: A deity added to Ninigi-no-Mikoto's company. Also called 櫛石窓神 and 豊石窓神 (readings unconfirmed), and regarded as a deity of the gates.

figures.name: Ame-no-Oshihi-no-Mikoto (天忍日命)
figures.role: Went at the front of Ninigi-no-Mikoto's company in arms together with Amatsukume-no-Mikoto. Ancestor of the Ōtomo no Muraji and others.

figures.name: Amatsukume-no-Mikoto (天津久米命)
figures.role: Went at the front of Ninigi-no-Mikoto's company in arms together with Ame-no-Oshihi-no-Mikoto. Ancestor of the Kume no Atai and others.

figures.name: Curved jewels, mirror and Kusanagi sword (八尺勾𤥼, 鏡, 草那藝釼)
figures.role: The jewels, mirror and sword given to Ninigi-no-Mikoto at the descent. The mirror was ordered to be worshipped as the spirit of Amaterasu-Ōmikami.

figures.name: Sokodoku-mitama (底度久御魂)
figures.role: The name of Sarutahiko-no-Kami when he sank into the sea at 阿耶訶 (reading unconfirmed) and reached the bottom.

figures.name: Tsubutatsu-mitama (都夫多都御魂)
figures.role: The name of Sarutahiko-no-Kami when, as he drowned, the sea water rose in bubbles.

figures.name: Awasaku-mitama (阿和佐久御魂)
figures.role: The name of Sarutahiko-no-Kami when, as he drowned, the foam burst.

figures.name: Sarume no Kimi (猿女君)
figures.role: A lineage descended from Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto. Their taking on the name of Sarutahiko-no-Kami is regarded as the origin of their name.

figures.name: Sea cucumber (海鼠, read ko)
figures.role: The only one that did not answer the question whether it would serve the Heavenly Grandson; its mouth was slit by Ame-no-Uzume-no-Mikoto.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 9, Takamimusubi-no-Mikoto (高皇産霊尊) covers the imperial grandson 天津火瓊瓊杵尊 (Ninigi) with a bed-covering (真床追衾) and sends him down. The story of the change from Ame-no-Oshihomimi-no-Mikoto (天忍穂耳尊) to his son, the story of the bestowal of the jewels, mirror and sword, and Sarutahiko do not appear.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, variant account 1
compare.text: In variant account 1 of section 9, Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神) gives the imperial grandson the “three treasures,” the Yasakani curved jewels (八坂瓊曲玉), the Yata mirror (八咫鏡) and the Kusanagi sword (草薙剣), together with the deities of the five groups (五部神), and Sarutahiko-no-Ōkami (猿田彦大神) comes out to meet him at the Eightfold Crossroads of Heaven (天八達之衢). Sarutahiko says that he will go to the upper reaches of the Isuzu River (五十鈴川) at 狭長田 (reading unconfirmed) in Ise.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, variant account 4
compare.text: In variant account 4 of section 9, Ame-no-Oshihi-no-Mikoto, the distant ancestor of the Ōtomo no Muraji, leads 天槵津大来目 (reading unconfirmed), the distant ancestor of the Kume-be (来目部), and goes ahead as guide. In the Kojiki, the two, Ame-no-Oshihi-no-Mikoto and Amatsukume-no-Mikoto, lead the way side by side.

konohana.title: Konohanasakuya-hime and Iwanagahime
konohana.lead: Ninigi-no-Mikoto, having come down from heaven, took as his wife Konohanasakuya-hime, daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, at the cape of 笠紗 (reading unconfirmed). But he sent back her elder sister Iwanagahime (石長比売), who had been offered together with her, as ugly, and the Kojiki says that this is why the lives of the emperors are not long. Sakuya-hime, suspected because she had conceived in a single night, gave birth to three children, Hoderi-no-Mikoto, Hosuseri-no-Mikoto and 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed), inside a birth hall that had been set on fire.

points.text: Because Ninigi-no-Mikoto sent back the elder sister Iwanagahime as ugly and took only the younger sister Konohanasakuya-hime as his wife, the lives of the children of the heavenly deity became as fleeting as the blossoms of trees, just as Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami had said. The Kojiki says that this is why, even now, the lives of the emperors are not long.

Konohanasakuya-hime, suspected by Ninigi-no-Mikoto because she had conceived in a single night, said, “If it is the child of the heavenly deity, it will be born safely,” entered a hall with no door, set it on fire and gave birth, bearing three children: Hoderi-no-Mikoto, Hosuseri-no-Mikoto and 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed).

Of the three born in the fire, the eldest, Hoderi-no-Mikoto, is noted in a small note as the ancestor of the 阿多君 (reading unconfirmed) of the Hayato, and the youngest, 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed; also called 天津日高日子穂穂手見命), becomes the hero of the story of Umisachi and Yamasachi (海幸山幸) that follows.

In variant account 2 of the Nihon Shoki, section 9, the shortening of life is attributed not to the father's vow but to the curse spoken by Iwanagahime (磐長姫) herself in her shame, and within it a “one version says” (一云) tells it as the origin of the fleeting lives not only of the emperors but of all people in the world.

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, this story, in which the stone is rejected and a short life is received, is regarded as belonging to a type of myth called the “Banana type,” found in Southeast Asia and elsewhere, and it is thought that a story originally about the origin of death for humans in general became attached to the myth of Ninigi-no-Mikoto.

The same database introduces the view that, through Ninigi-no-Mikoto marrying the daughter of a mountain deity and his son 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) marrying the daughter of a sea deity, the descendants of the heavenly deity take in the powers of both mountain and sea, which carries the meaning that they gain the qualification to rule the earth.

story.text: 天津日高日子番能邇邇藝能命 (Ninigi-no-Mikoto) met a beautiful woman at the cape of 笠紗 (reading unconfirmed). When he asked whose daughter she was, she answered that she was a daughter of Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, named Kamuatatsu-hime (神阿多都比売), also called Konohanasakuya-hime. When he asked whether she had sisters, she answered that she had an elder sister, Iwanagahime (石長比売). When Ninigi-no-Mikoto said he wished to take her as his wife, Sakuya-hime said, “I cannot answer on my own. My father, Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, will answer.”

So he sent a messenger to her father Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, who was greatly pleased and offered her together with her elder sister Iwanagahime, sending them with many goods laden on stands. But because the elder sister was very ugly, Ninigi-no-Mikoto was frightened when he saw her and sent her back. He kept only the younger sister, Konohanasakuya-hime, and spent one night with her.

Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, deeply ashamed that Iwanagahime had been sent back, sent word as follows. He had offered his two daughters together because he had sworn a vow: if Iwanagahime were kept at his side, the life of the child of the heavenly deity would remain unmoving forever like a rock, even when snow falls and wind blows; and if Konohanasakuya-hime were kept at his side, he would flourish as the blossoms of trees bloom. Since he had sent back Iwanagahime and kept only Sakuya-hime, the life of the child of the heavenly deity would be as fleeting as the blossoms of trees. The Kojiki records that for this reason, down to the present, the lives of the emperors are not long.

Later Sakuya-hime came and said, “I am with child, and the birth is near. Since it is the child of the heavenly deity, I cannot give birth to it by myself as I please.” Ninigi-no-Mikoto then said, “You conceived in a single night? That is not my child. Surely it is the child of an earthly deity.” Sakuya-hime answered, “If the child I carry is the child of an earthly deity, it will not be born safely. If it is the child of the heavenly deity, it will be born safely.”

Sakuya-hime built a large hall with no doorway (無戸八尋殿), went inside, and sealed it up with clay. Then, at the time of the birth, she set fire to the hall and gave birth. The child born when the fire was blazing fiercely was Hoderi-no-Mikoto (a small note says he is the ancestor of the 阿多君 (reading unconfirmed) of the Hayato), next Hosuseri-no-Mikoto, and next 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed), whose other name is 天津日高日子穂穂手見命 (Hikohohodemi).

quotes.note: (Sending back the elder sister,) he kept only the younger sister, Konohanasakuya-hime, and spent one night with her.
(If Iwanagahime were kept at his side, the life of the child of the heavenly deity) would always remain firm and unmoving like a rock, even when snow falls and wind blows.
For this reason, down to the present, the lives of the emperors are not long.
If (the child I carry) is the child of the heavenly deity, it will be born safely.

figures.name: Hoderi-no-Mikoto (火照命)
figures.role: The first child named in the burning birth hall; a small note says he is the ancestor of the 阿多君 (reading unconfirmed) of the Hayato.

figures.name: Hosuseri-no-Mikoto (火須勢理命)
figures.role: The child born after Hoderi-no-Mikoto in the burning birth hall.

figures.name: Doorless hall (無戸八尋殿)
figures.role: The large hall with no doorway that Sakuya-hime built for the birth; she sealed it with clay, set it on fire and gave birth inside it.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, variant account 2
compare.text: Variant account 2 of section 9 also has the story of the elder sister Iwanagahime (磐長姫) being rejected as ugly, but the shortening of life is attributed to Iwanagahime's curse in her shame, and its “one version says” (一云) makes it the origin of the fleeting lives of people in general (“顯見蒼生”). In the Kojiki it results from the vow of the father, Ōyamatsumi-no-Kami, and it is a story about the lives of the emperors.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: Iwanagahime does not appear in the main text of section 9; the wife's name is 鹿葦津姫 (reading unconfirmed), and a small note gives her other names as 神吾田津姫 (reading unconfirmed) and Konohanasakuya-hime (木花之開耶姫). The points that she is suspected for conceiving in a single night and gives birth after setting fire to a doorless chamber (無戸室) are shared with the Kojiki.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 9, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 9, the children born are three: Honosusori-no-Mikoto (火闌降命), Hikohohodemi-no-Mikoto (彦火火出見尊) and Hoakari-no-Mikoto (火明命), and Honosusori-no-Mikoto, born first, is noted in a small note as the first ancestor of the Hayato and others. In the Kojiki, the ancestor of the 阿多君 (reading unconfirmed) of the Hayato is Hoderi-no-Mikoto, and the third child is 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed).

umisachi.title: Umisachi and Yamasachi (海幸山幸)
umisachi.lead: The younger brother 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed; Yamasachibiko, 山佐知毘古) lost in the sea the fishhook he had borrowed from his elder brother Hoderi-no-Mikoto (Umisachibiko, 海佐知毘古). With the help of Shiotsuchi-no-Kami (塩椎神) he went to the palace of Watatsumi-no-Kami (綿津見神), married Toyotama-hime, and spent three years there. Having recovered the fishhook with the sea deity's help, 火遠理命 subdued his elder brother with the tide-raising jewel and the tide-ebbing jewel he had been given, and the elder brother swore to serve him as a guard by day and by night.

points.text: 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed; Yamasachibiko) exchanged tools with his elder brother Hoderi-no-Mikoto (Umisachibiko), but lost the fishhook in the sea. The elder brother would not accept even a thousand fishhooks made from a sword and demanded the original fishhook, so 火遠理命 set out for the palace of Watatsumi-no-Kami in the small boat of Shiotsuchi-no-Kami.

At the sea deity's palace, 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) married Toyotama-hime and lived there for three years. The sea deity, hearing the reason for his coming, gathered the fish of the sea and found the fishhook in the 赤海鯽魚 (reading unconfirmed), a fish whose throat was sore.

The sea deity gave him the tide-raising jewel (塩盈珠) and the tide-ebbing jewel (塩乾珠) together with the fishhook. Returning to the land, 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) used them to make his elder brother drown and then to save him, and Hoderi-no-Mikoto, surrendering, swore to serve as a guard by day and by night.

The origin story is told that the one-fathom wani, Hitohiro-wani (一尋和迩), which carried 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) back to the land in a single day, came to be called Sahimochi-no-Kami (佐比持神) because a small sword on a cord was fastened to its neck.

In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, section 10, the elder brother is named Honosusori-no-Mikoto (火闌降命); Shiotsuchi-no-Oji (鹽土老翁) puts Hohodemi-no-Mikoto (火火出見尊) not in a boat but in a basket without gaps (無目篭) and sinks it in the sea; and the surrendering elder brother swears to become one of the “people who perform as entertainers” (俳優之民).

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, the ending in which the elder brother submits to the younger is regarded as a story explaining the origin of the fact that, at the time of compilation, the Hayato guarded the court and served with the Hayato dance (隼人舞) and the like. It is also pointed out that the plot of going to another world to search for a lost fishhook resembles tales of the “Lost Fishhook type” found in Indonesia and elsewhere.

story.text: Hoderi-no-Mikoto, as Umisachibiko, caught the fish of the sea, and 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed), as Yamasachibiko, caught the beasts of the mountains. 火遠理命 asked his elder brother three times, “Let us exchange our sachi (佐知; tools for catching game) and use them,” and at last the exchange was made. But though he fished in the sea, he did not catch a single fish, and moreover he lost the fishhook in the sea. When his elder brother demanded the fishhook back, the younger brother broke up the ten-fist sword (十拳剣) at his waist and made five hundred fishhooks, and then made a thousand fishhooks, to make amends, but the elder brother would not accept them and said, “I still want the original fishhook.”

As 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) was weeping by the seashore, Shiotsuchi-no-Kami (塩椎神) came and asked him why. Hearing the circumstances, Shiotsuchi-no-Kami built a small, tightly woven boat with no gaps (无間勝間之小船), put 火遠理命 in it, and instructed him: “I will push this boat off. Go on for a while and there will be a good path. If you follow that path, you will reach a palace built like the scales of a fish, the palace of Watatsumi-no-Kami. Above the well beside the gate there is a sacred katsura tree (湯津香木). If you sit up in that tree, the daughter of the sea deity will see to things for you.”

When he sat up in the tree as instructed, a maidservant of Toyotama-hime, coming to draw water with a jewelled vessel, noticed a light in the well, looked up, and saw a handsome man. 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) asked for water, but instead of drinking it he took a jewel from his necklace into his mouth and spat it into the vessel. The jewel stuck to the vessel and would not come off, so the maidservant presented it as it was to Toyotama-hime. Toyotama-hime came out to look, was drawn to him, and told her father. The sea deity said, “This is the child of 天津日高 (reading unconfirmed), 虚空津日高 (reading unconfirmed),” welcomed him into the palace, entertained him generously, and gave him his daughter in marriage. 火遠理命 lived in that land for three years.

One night 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) remembered how it had all begun and heaved a great sigh. Hearing of it from Toyotama-hime, the sea deity asked him the reason, and 火遠理命 told how he had lost his elder brother's fishhook and been reproached. When the sea deity called together all the fish of the sea, large and small, and questioned them, the fish said, “The 赤海鯽魚 (reading unconfirmed) is complaining that something is stuck in its throat and it cannot eat.” When they searched the throat of the 赤海鯽魚, there was the fishhook.

The sea deity washed the fishhook and handed it to 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed), instructing him that when he returned it to his elder brother he should say “淤煩鉤”, “須須鉤”, “貧鉤”, “宇流鉤” and hand it over behind his back. He also said: if your elder brother makes his rice fields on high ground, make yours on low ground; if he makes them on low ground, make yours on high ground. Since I govern the waters, within three years your elder brother will become poor. Then he instructed him that if the elder brother, resentful, attacked him, he should bring out the tide-raising jewel (塩盈珠) and drown him, and if he begged forgiveness, he should bring out the tide-ebbing jewel (塩乾珠) and save him, and he gave him the two jewels.

When the sea deity gathered the wani (和迩) and asked who could carry him back and in how many days, the one-fathom wani, Hitohiro-wani (一尋和迩), offered, “I will carry him in one day and come back.” 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) rode on its neck and was carried back within a single day, and when the wani was returning, he fastened a small sword on a cord to its neck; therefore this one-fathom wani is called Sahimochi-no-Kami (佐比持神) to this day. When he did as instructed, his elder brother gradually became poor and attacked him with a violent heart, but 火遠理命 drowned him with the tide-raising jewel, and when he begged forgiveness, saved him with the tide-ebbing jewel. The elder brother, suffering, bowed his head and swore that from then on he would serve as a guard by day and by night, and it is recorded that, down to the present, they serve by constantly performing the various gestures he made when he was drowning.

quotes.note: (However many fishhooks were made in amends,) the elder brother said, “I still want the original fishhook.”
A palace built like the scales of a fish: that is the palace of Watatsumi-no-Kami (the instruction of Shiotsuchi-no-Kami).
(If your elder brother attacks,) bring out the tide-raising jewel and drown him; if he begs forgiveness, bring out the tide-ebbing jewel and let him live (the instruction of the sea deity).
I will serve you as a guard by day and by night (the oath of the surrendering elder brother).

figures.name: Hoderi-no-Mikoto (Umisachibiko) (火照命（海佐知毗古）)
figures.role: The elder brother who catches the fish of the sea. He reproaches his younger brother to return the fishhook he lent, and in the end surrenders to his younger brother and swears to serve him.

figures.name: Small tightly woven boat (无間勝間之小船)
figures.role: The small boat built by Shiotsuchi-no-Kami, in which he put 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) and sent him toward the palace of Watatsumi-no-Kami.

figures.name: Yutsu-katsura (湯津香木)
figures.role: The tree above the well beside the gate of the palace of Watatsumi-no-Kami; 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) sat in it and was found by Toyotama-hime's maidservant (a reading note says “香木” is read 加都良, katsura).

figures.name: 赤海鯽魚 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The fish in whose throat the fishhook of 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) was stuck.

figures.name: Tide-raising jewel and tide-ebbing jewel (塩盈珠, 塩乾珠)
figures.role: The two jewels the sea deity gave 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed); with the tide-raising jewel he made his elder brother drown, and with the tide-ebbing jewel he saved him.

figures.name: Hitohiro-wani (Sahimochi-no-Kami) (一尋和迩（佐比持神）)
figures.role: Carried 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) on its neck back to the land in one day, had a small sword on a cord fastened to it, and came to be called Sahimochi-no-Kami.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 10, main text
compare.text: In the main text of the Shoki, Shiotsuchi-no-Oji (鹽土老翁) makes not a boat but a basket without gaps (無目篭), puts Hohodemi-no-Mikoto (火火出見尊) inside it, and sinks it in the sea. In the Kojiki, Shiotsuchi-no-Kami (塩椎神) builds the small boat 无間勝間之小船, puts him in it and pushes it off.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 10, main text
compare.text: In the main text of the Shoki, the one holding the fishhook is 赤女 (reading unconfirmed; a small note says it is a name for the sea bream), who did not come to the gathering because of a mouth ailment. In the Kojiki, the 赤海鯽魚 (reading unconfirmed) complains that something is stuck in its throat and it cannot eat.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 10, main text
compare.text: In the main text of the Shoki, the surrendering elder brother, Honosusori-no-Mikoto (火闌降命), swears, “I will become your people who perform as entertainers (俳優之民),” and he is regarded as the ancestor of 吾田君小橋 (reading unconfirmed) and others. In the Kojiki, the elder brother is Hoderi-no-Mikoto, and he swears to serve as a guard by day and by night.

ugaya.title: The Birth of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto
ugaya.lead: Toyotama-hime, daughter of the sea deity, came to the land and gave birth to a child in a birth hall whose roof was only partly thatched with cormorant feathers. But her plea “Do not look” was broken, she was seen in the form of an eight-fathom wani (八尋和迩), and she closed off the sea boundary (海坂) and returned to the land of the sea. The child born, Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto, later took his aunt Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto (玉依毘売命) as his wife and had four children, including 若御毛沼命 (reading unconfirmed; 神倭伊波礼毗古命).

points.text: Toyotama-hime asked him “Do not look,” but when 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) peeked, she was crawling and writhing in the form of an eight-fathom wani (八尋和迩), so he fled. Ashamed, Toyotama-hime left the child behind, closed off the sea boundary (海坂) and returned to the land of the sea.
Because he was born before the roof of the birth hall on the seashore, being thatched with cormorant feathers, was finished, the child was named 天津日高日子波限建鵜葺草葺不合命 (Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto).

Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto took his aunt Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto (玉依毘売命) as his wife and had four children: Itsuse-no-Mikoto, Inahi-no-Mikoto, 御毛沼命 (reading unconfirmed) and 若御毛沼命 (reading unconfirmed). The youngest, 若御毛沼命, is also called 神倭伊波礼毗古命 (reading unconfirmed).

Even after their parting, Toyotama-hime, out of longing, sent a song entrusted to her younger sister Tamayori-hime (玉依毘売), and 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) answered in a song that he would never forget his wife as long as he lived. It is recorded that 火遠理命 remained at the Takachiho palace for five hundred and eighty years.

In the main text of the Nihon Shoki, section 10, Toyotama-hime (豊玉姫) takes the form of a dragon at the time of the birth, wraps the child in grass, leaves it on the seashore and departs. In variant account 1 she has the form of an eight-fathom great 熊鰐 (reading unconfirmed; 八尋大熊鰐), and in variant account 3 that of an eight-fathom great 鰐 (reading unconfirmed; 八尋大鰐).

According to the Kokugakuin University database of deity names, the influential view is that this story, in which a wife whose “do not look” promise is broken leaves for her original world, is one of the stories of non-human wives called the “Melusine type,” found widely around the world. There is also a view that the scene of closing off the sea boundary tells the origin of why the sea and the land can no longer be travelled between, and serves to close the world of myth at the end of Part 1.

story.text: Toyotama-hime-no-Mikoto, daughter of the sea deity, came to the land of her own accord and said, “I am with child, and the birth is near. I thought that the child of the heavenly deity should not be born in the sea plain, and so I have come.” So at the water's edge on the seashore a birth hall was built, using cormorant feathers as the thatch for its roof. But before the roof had been fully thatched, unable to bear the sudden pains, Toyotama-hime entered the birth hall.

When the time came to give birth, Toyotama-hime said to her husband, “People of other lands, when they give birth, take the form of their home land to give birth. So I too will now give birth in my original form. Please do not look at me.” 火遠理命 (reading unconfirmed) found these words strange, and secretly peeked as she was about to give birth. Then he saw that Toyotama-hime had become an eight-fathom wani (八尋和迩) and was crawling and writhing, and in astonishment and fear he fled.

Toyotama-hime, knowing she had been spied upon, felt ashamed. Leaving the child she had borne, she said, “I had always wished to come and go by the sea road. But to have my form spied upon is a great shame,” and she closed off the sea boundary (海坂) and went back to the sea. The child thus born was named 天津日高日子波限建鵜葺草葺不合命 (Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto). A reading note says that “波限” is read 那藝佐 (nagisa) and “葺草” is read 加夜 (kaya).

Afterwards, though Toyotama-hime resented his spying heart, she could not suppress her longing, and, on the occasion of having the child raised, she entrusted a song to her younger sister Tamayori-hime (玉依毘売) and sent it. The song said that while she was touched by the gleam of red jewels, the form of her husband, like white jewels, seemed precious to her. Her husband sang in reply that he would never forget, as long as he lived, the wife with whom he had slept on the island where the wild ducks, birds of the open sea, come to shore.

日子穂穂手見命 (Hikohohodemi; 火遠理命) remained at the Takachiho palace for five hundred and eighty years, and his tomb is to the west of the mountain of Takachiho. 天津日高日子波限建鵜葺草葺不合命 (Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto) took his aunt Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto as his wife and had four children: Itsuse-no-Mikoto, Inahi-no-Mikoto, 御毛沼命 (reading unconfirmed) and 若御毛沼命 (reading unconfirmed). 若御毛沼命 is also called 豊御毛沼命 (reading unconfirmed) and 神倭伊波礼毗古命 (reading unconfirmed). 御毛沼命 crossed over to Tokoyo-no-Kuni (常世国), treading on the crests of the waves, and Inahi-no-Mikoto entered the sea plain, as his mother's land (the original reads “妣國”).

quotes.note: The child of the heavenly deity should not be born in the sea plain (the reason Toyotama-hime came to the land).
(When he peeked, Toyotama-hime) had taken the form of a wani eight fathoms long, and was crawling and writhing.
So she closed off the boundary of the sea (海坂) and went back to the sea.
(The) other name (of 若御毛沼命) is 神倭伊波礼毗古命 (readings unconfirmed).

figures.name: Itsuse-no-Mikoto (五瀬命)
figures.role: The first child born to Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto and Tamayori-hime-no-Mikoto.

figures.name: Inahi-no-Mikoto (稲氷命)
figures.role: The second child of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto; he entered the sea plain as his mother's land.

figures.name: Birth hall (産殿)
figures.role: Built at the water's edge on the seashore with cormorant feathers as thatch; Toyotama-hime gave birth here before the roof was fully thatched.

figures.name: Yahiro-wani (八尋和迩)
figures.role: Toyotama-hime's original form, which she had taken at the time of the birth; being seen in it led to their parting.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 10, main text
compare.text: In the main text of the Shoki, Toyotama-hime (豊玉姫) is said to take the form of a dragon at the time of the birth. In the Kojiki it is the form of an eight-fathom wani (八尋和迩).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 10, main text
compare.text: In the main text of the Shoki, Toyotama-hime wraps the child in grass, abandons it on the seashore, closes the sea road and departs. In the Kojiki, she leaves the child she has borne, closes off the sea boundary (海坂) and returns, and later sends her younger sister Tamayori-hime to raise him.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 2, section 11, main text
compare.text: In the main text of section 11 of the Shoki as well, Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto (波瀲武鸕鷀草葺不合尊) takes his aunt Tamayori-hime (玉依姫) as his consort and has four sons, Itsuse-no-Mikoto (五瀨命), 稻飯命 (reading unconfirmed), Mikeirino-no-Mikoto (三毛入野命) and 神日本磐余尊 (reading unconfirmed); but it further records that he died at the 西洲之宮 (reading unconfirmed) and was buried at the 吾平山上陵 (reading unconfirmed) in Hyūga. The corresponding part of the Kojiki has no account of the death or tomb of Ugayafukiaezu-no-Mikoto.

jinmu-tosei.title: Emperor Jinmu's Eastern Expedition (from Hyūga to Kumano and Yoshino)
jinmu-tosei.lead: 神倭伊波禮毘古命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Jinmu) sets out east from the Takachiho palace in Hyūga together with his elder brother Itsuse-no-Mikoto, but in the battle with 登美能那賀須泥毘古 (reading unconfirmed) Itsuse-no-Mikoto is wounded by an arrow and dies at the 男水門 (reading unconfirmed) in Kii. In Kumano, the party overcomes danger thanks to a sword sent down from heaven and to the guidance of Yatagarasu (八咫烏), sent by 高木大神 (reading unconfirmed), and, meeting the earthly deities of Yoshino along the way, enters Uda.

points.text: Itsuse-no-Mikoto was wounded in the hand by an arrow of 登美毘古 (reading unconfirmed) and, saying that “it was wrong for the child of the sun deity to fight facing the sun,” chose a route circling round to the south so as to have the sun at their backs. On the way he died at the 男之水門 (reading unconfirmed) in the land of Kii (紀国), and it is recorded that his tomb is at 竈山 (reading unconfirmed).

In Kumano, when the party had fallen prostrate, the violent deities were cut down by a sword presented by 高倉下 (reading unconfirmed), and the troops awoke.
