As he was dying, 熊曾建 (reading unconfirmed) offered him the name "倭建御子" (Prince Yamato Takeru), and from then on 小碓命 (倭男具那王) (reading unconfirmed) was called Yamato Takeru (倭建命).
In Izumo on the way back, he became friends with Izumo Takeru (出雲建), made him exchange his own sword for a fake sword of 赤檮 wood (詐刀), and struck down Izumo Takeru, who could not draw the fake sword.

In the Nihon Shoki, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (日本武尊) goes to attack the Kumaso in the 10th month of the 27th year of Emperor Keikō, at the age of sixteen, and the one he strikes down is 川上梟帥 (reading unconfirmed) alone. The story of Izumo Takeru is not in the Keikō chapter; a similar killing by deceit using a wooden sword appears in the 60th year of Emperor Sujin as the story of 出雲振根 (reading unconfirmed).

Concerning the "Anato-no-Kami" (穴戸神) whom he subdued (言向) on the way back, the Kokugakuin University deity-name database introduces the view that it is 穴門 (reading unconfirmed) in Nagato Province, the view that it is 穴海 (reading unconfirmed) in Kibi Province, and the view that it is a word for straits in general and not a proper noun. The Nihon Shoki says that on this return journey he killed the evil deities of 穴濟 in Kibi and of 柏濟 in Naniwa (reading unconfirmed).

story.text: Emperor Keikō ruled the realm from the 日代宮 of 纒向 (reading unconfirmed). He married 針間之伊那毘能大郎女 (reading unconfirmed), and 櫛角別王, 大碓命, 小碓命 (also named 倭男具那命), 倭根子命 and 神櫛王 (reading unconfirmed) were born. His children numbered eighty in all: twenty-one recorded princes and princesses and fifty-nine not recorded. Three of them, 若帶日子命, Yamato Takeru (倭建命) and 五百木之入日子命 (reading unconfirmed), bore the title of crown prince, and the remaining seventy-seven were distributed among the provinces as governors (國造), 和氣, 稻置 and district chiefs (縣主). The original text first sums up that 若帶日子命 ruled the realm and that 小碓命 subdued the unruly deities and the unsubmissive people of east and west.

The emperor heard that the two daughters of 神大根王 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the governors of 三野國 (reading unconfirmed), 兄比賣 and 弟比賣 (reading unconfirmed), were beautiful, and sent 大碓命 (reading unconfirmed) to bring them to court. But 大碓命 did not bring the two to court; he took them as his own wives, found other women, and presented them falsely under their names. The emperor knew they were other women and did not marry them (original text: "恒令經長眼。亦勿婚而惚也"). In this reign the 田部, the 淡水門 of the east, the 膳之大伴部 and the 倭屯家 (reading unconfirmed) were established, and the 坂手 Pond (reading unconfirmed) was made.

The emperor asked 小碓命 (reading unconfirmed) why his elder brother did not come out to the morning and evening imperial meals, and ordered him to "泥疑" (reading unconfirmed) him and teach him. When five days had passed and his brother still did not come out, the emperor asked, and 小碓命 answered that he had already "泥疑"-ed him. Asked how he had done it, he answered that at dawn, when his brother went into the privy, he had lain in wait, seized him and crushed him, torn off his limbs, wrapped him in a straw mat and thrown him away. The emperor feared his son's fierce and violent heart and sent him to strike down the two 熊曾建 (reading unconfirmed) in the west, who were unsubmissive and lacking in respect. At this time 小碓命's hair was still tied up on his forehead.

小碓命 (reading unconfirmed) received a robe and a skirt from his aunt 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed), put a small sword in the fold of his garment, and set out. When he reached the house of the 熊曾建 (reading unconfirmed) and looked, an army surrounded the house in three rings, and the 熊曾建 had built a chamber (室) and were in it, clamoring that they would hold a "御室樂" (reading unconfirmed) feast and preparing food. On the day of the feast, 小碓命 combed down his tied-up hair like a young girl's, put on his aunt's robe and skirt, took on the appearance of a young girl, and entered the chamber mixed among the women. The 熊曾建 brothers were charmed by this girl, seated her between the two of them, and made merry.

When the feast was at its height, 小碓命 (reading unconfirmed) drew the sword from the fold of his garment, seized 熊曾建 (reading unconfirmed) by the collar of his clothes and stabbed him through the chest. The younger 建 fled in fear, but 小碓命 chased him to the "椅本" (reading unconfirmed) of the chamber, seized him by the back, and stabbed the sword through him from the buttocks. 熊曾建 said, "Do not move the sword; I have something to say," and asked his name. When 小碓命 declared that he was 倭男具那王 (reading unconfirmed), son of the emperor who rules the Great Land of Eight Islands (大八嶋國) from the 日代宮 of 纒向 (reading unconfirmed), 熊曾建 said that in the west there was no one stronger than the two of them, but that in the land of Great Yamato (大倭國) there was a strong man who surpassed them, and he offered the name "倭建御子" (Prince Yamato Takeru). When he had finished speaking, 小碓命 cut him down as one splits a ripe melon, and from this time he was called Yamato Takeru (倭建命).

On the way back to the capital, Yamato Takeru subdued and pacified (言向和) all the mountain deities, the river deities and Anato-no-Kami (穴戸神). On entering the province of Izumo, intending to kill Izumo Takeru (出雲建), he first became his friend, and secretly made a fake sword (詐刀) of 赤檮 (reading unconfirmed) wood and wore it. When the two bathed in the 肥河 (reading unconfirmed), Yamato Takeru came up out of the river first, took and put on the sword that Izumo Takeru had untied and laid aside, and said, "Let us exchange swords." When Izumo Takeru, coming up afterwards, put on Yamato Takeru's fake sword, Yamato Takeru challenged him to cross swords; Izumo Takeru could not draw the fake sword and was struck down by Yamato Takeru. Yamato Takeru composed a song at this time, and having thus pacified the land, he returned to the capital and reported.

quotes.note: The answer of 小碓命 (reading unconfirmed): at dawn, when his brother went into the privy, he seized him and crushed him, tore off his limbs, wrapped him in a straw mat and threw him away.
He put on his aunt's robe and skirt and took on the full appearance of a young girl.
The words of 熊曾建 (reading unconfirmed): "I will offer you a name. From now on it is fitting that you be called 倭建御子 (Prince Yamato Takeru)."

figures.name: 大帶日子淤斯呂和氣天皇 (reading unconfirmed) (Emperor Keikō)
figures.role: The emperor of this story. Fearing the violence of 小碓命, he sent him to subdue the 熊曾建 in the west.

figures.name: 大碓命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Elder brother of 小碓命. He took as his own wives 兄比賣 and 弟比賣, whom the emperor intended to summon, and was later killed by 小碓命.

figures.name: 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Aunt of 小碓命. She gave him the robe and skirt used for his disguise.

figures.name: 熊曾建 (two brothers) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Brothers struck down as unsubmissive people in the west. The younger, as he was dying, offered the name "倭建".

figures.name: Izumo Takeru (出雲建)
figures.role: A figure of Izumo. He became friends with Yamato Takeru, but was tricked into taking a fake sword and was struck down.

figures.name: Anato-no-Kami (穴戸神)
figures.role: A deity subdued by Yamato Takeru, together with the mountain deities and river deities, on the way back from the western campaign.

figures.name: Fake sword (詐刀, made of 赤檮 wood) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: An undrawable wooden sword that Yamato Takeru made to deceive Izumo Takeru.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 27th year of Emperor Keikō, winter, 10th month (丁酉朔己酉)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, because the Kumaso rebelled again, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (日本武尊) was sent in the 10th month of the 27th year of Emperor Keikō, and he was sixteen at the time. Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto takes with him 弟彦公 (reading unconfirmed), a master archer of Mino, and others. The Kojiki's account, in which the killing of his elder brother 大碓命 (reading unconfirmed) was what led to his dispatch, does not appear in this entry.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 27th year of Emperor Keikō, 12th month
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the one struck down is the Kumaso chief 取石鹿文 (川上梟帥) (reading unconfirmed) alone, and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto untied his hair and entered the feasting chamber in the guise of a young girl. As he was dying, 川上梟帥 offered him the title "日本武皇子" (Prince Yamato Takeru).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 5 — the 60th year of Emperor Sujin, autumn, 7th month (丙申朔己酉)
compare.text: There is no story of Izumo Takeru in the Keikō chapter. In the Sujin chapter there is a story in which 出雲振根 (reading unconfirmed) makes a wooden sword, bathes with his younger brother 飯入根 at the 止屋淵 (reading unconfirmed), exchanges it for a real sword and kills his brother; the song of the people of the time also begins with words closely resembling Yamato Takeru's song in the Kojiki.

yamatotakeru-tosei.title: The Eastern Campaign of Yamato Takeru (倭建命)
yamatotakeru-tosei.lead: Ordered to pacify the twelve circuits of the east (東方十二道) soon after returning from the western campaign, Yamato Takeru (倭建命) lamented to his aunt 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) at Ise and received from her the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劍) and a bag (御嚢). He came through a grass fire in 相武國 (reading unconfirmed); at the 走水海 (reading unconfirmed) sea his consort 弟橘比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) entered the sea in his place; and on the 足柄 (reading unconfirmed) slope he lamented "阿豆麻波夜" (reading unconfirmed) before reaching the 酒折宮 (reading unconfirmed) in Kai.

points.text: Ordered to pacify the twelve circuits of the east, Yamato Takeru (倭建命) lamented and wept to his aunt 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) at Ise, saying, "The emperor has my death in mind," and was given the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劍) and a bag (御嚢).

In 相武國 (reading unconfirmed), deceived by the governor (國造) and surrounded by a grass fire, Yamato Takeru cut the grass with his sword, lit a counter-fire with the fire-striker in the bag, escaped, and destroyed the governor and his men. This is regarded as the origin of the place name 燒津 (reading unconfirmed).

When the crossing deity (渡神) of the 走水海 (reading unconfirmed) sea raised the waves, his consort 弟橘比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) spread mats on the waves and entered the sea; the waves calmed and the ship could go on. Seven days later the consort's comb washed ashore, and a tomb was made in which it was laid.

On the 足柄 (reading unconfirmed) slope Yamato Takeru struck dead the slope deity, who had become a white deer, with a piece of 蒜 (garlic); then at the top of the slope he lamented three times, "阿豆麻波夜" (reading unconfirmed). This is regarded as the origin of the name "阿豆麻" for that land.

In the Nihon Shoki (the 40th year of Emperor Keikō), Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (日本武尊) volunteered on his own to take on the eastern campaign; he meets the grass fire in Suruga, laments "吾嬬者耶" (reading unconfirmed) at the 碓日嶺 (reading unconfirmed) pass, and kills the mountain deity in the form of a white deer with garlic (蒜) in the mountains of Shinano.

The Kokugakuin University deity-name database (entry for Shinano-no-Saka-no-Kami, 科野之坂神) notes that it has been pointed out that the story in the Nihon Shoki, in which the mountain deity of the slope in Shinano becomes a white deer and is killed with garlic, closely resembles the Kojiki story of the deity of the 足柄 (reading unconfirmed) slope.

story.text: The emperor again ordered Yamato Takeru (倭建命) to subdue and pacify (言向和) the unruly deities and unsubmissive people of the twelve circuits of the east (東方十二道). He assigned 御鉏友耳建日子 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 吉備臣 (reading unconfirmed) and others, to accompany him, and gave him the eight-fathom spear of 比比羅木 (reading unconfirmed). On setting out, Yamato Takeru went to the Great Shrine of Ise (伊勢大御神宮) and said to his aunt 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed), "Does the emperor think I should die? I have only just returned from striking down the evil men of the west, and yet without even giving me an army he now sends me again to pacify the evil men of the twelve circuits of the east. Surely he wishes for my death," and he lamented and wept. 倭比賣命 gave him the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劍), and also gave him a bag (御嚢), telling him to untie its mouth if anything urgent happened.

On reaching Owari, Yamato Takeru entered the house of Miyazu-hime (美夜受比賣), ancestor of the governors of Owari (尾張國造). He intended to marry her, but thinking again that he would marry her on his way back, he made a promise with her and headed for the eastern provinces, subduing and pacifying the unruly deities of the mountains and rivers and the unsubmissive people. When he reached 相武國 (reading unconfirmed), its governor (國造) falsely told him, "In the middle of this plain there is a large marsh, and a very violent deity lives there." When Yamato Takeru entered the plain to see that deity, the governor set fire to the plain.

Realizing he had been deceived, Yamato Takeru opened the mouth of the bag given him by 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) and looked, and there was a fire-striker inside. First he cut away the grass with his sword, then struck fire with the fire-striker and lit a counter-fire, burned back the approaching fire, and came out of the plain. He then cut down and destroyed all the governor and his men and set fire to them and burned them, so that place is still called 燒津 (reading unconfirmed).

Going on from there, he was about to cross the 走水海 (reading unconfirmed) sea when the crossing deity (渡神) raised the waves and spun the ship round and round so that it could not go forward. His consort 弟橘比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) offered, "I will enter the sea in place of the prince. Let the prince accomplish the task he was sent on and report to the emperor." She spread mats of sedge (菅疊), of hide (皮疊) and of silk (絁疊), each eightfold, on the waves and stepped down onto them. Then the rough waves calmed of themselves, and the ship was able to go on. At this time the consort composed a song.

Seven days later the consort's comb washed up on the shore, so the comb was taken, a tomb was made, and the comb was laid in it. Yamato Takeru went further, subdued all the unruly Emishi (蝦夷), pacified the unruly deities of the mountains and rivers, and started home. When he was eating at the foot of the 足柄 (reading unconfirmed) slope, the slope deity appeared, having become a white deer, and stood there; he struck it with a leftover scrap of 蒜 (garlic), hit it in the eye, and killed it.

Yamato Takeru climbed to the top of the slope, stood there and lamented three times, saying, "阿豆麻波夜" (reading unconfirmed). Therefore that land is called 阿豆麻. Crossing from there into Kai, while he was at the 酒折宮 (reading unconfirmed), Yamato Takeru composed a song, and an old man who was tending the fires (御火) continued the song with one of his own.

quotes.note: Yamato Takeru's words to 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed): "Does the emperor now think I should die?"
When he opened the mouth of the bag given him by his aunt 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed), there was a fire-striker inside.
The words of 弟橘比賣命 (reading unconfirmed): "I will enter the sea in place of the prince."
At the top of the 足柄 (reading unconfirmed) slope he lamented three times, saying, "阿豆麻波夜". This is regarded as the origin of the name 阿豆麻.

figures.name: 倭比賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Aunt of Yamato Takeru. At Ise she heard his lament and gave him the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劍) and the bag (御嚢).

figures.name: 御鉏友耳建日子 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Ancestor of the 吉備臣 and others. He was sent to accompany the eastern campaign.

figures.name: The eight-fathom spear of 比比羅木 (比比羅木之八尋矛) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The spear the emperor gave Yamato Takeru as he set out on the eastern campaign.

figures.name: The Kusanagi sword (草那藝劍)
figures.role: The sword given by 倭比賣命. At the grass fire in 相武國, Yamato Takeru first cut away the grass with his sword.

figures.name: The bag (御嚢, with the fire-striker)
figures.role: The bag given by 倭比賣命. With the fire-striker inside, he lit a counter-fire and escaped the grass fire.

figures.name: The governor of 相武國 (相武國造) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: He falsely said that an unruly deity lived in a marsh on the plain, lured Yamato Takeru onto the plain, and set it on fire.

figures.name: The crossing deity of the 走水海 sea (走水海渡神) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The deity who raised the waves and stopped Yamato Takeru's ship from going forward.

figures.name: 弟橘比賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Consort of Yamato Takeru. She entered the sea in his place and calmed the rough waves.

figures.name: The deity of the 足柄 slope (足柄之坂神, white deer) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The slope deity who appeared in the form of a white deer and was struck dead with garlic (蒜) by Yamato Takeru.

figures.name: The old man who tended the fires (御火燒之老人)
figures.role: The old man who, at the 酒折宮, continued Yamato Takeru's song with one of his own.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 40th year of Emperor Keikō, autumn, 7th month (癸未朔戊戌)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, when the ministers could not decide whom to send against the rebellion in the east, Prince 大碓 (reading unconfirmed) ran away and hid, whereas Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (日本武尊) took on the pacification himself; the emperor gave him an axe of authority (斧鉞) and said, "In form you are my son, but in truth you are a divine man." There is no scene, as in the Kojiki, in which Yamato Takeru laments that "my father wishes for my death."

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 40th year of Emperor Keikō, winter, 10th month (戊午), and "this year" (是歳)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, what 倭姫命 (reading unconfirmed) gives him at Ise is only the Kusanagi sword (草薙釼), and he meets the grass fire in Suruga. In the main text he lights a counter-fire with a fire-striker (燧) and escapes; an alternative account (一云) relates that the 叢雲 (reading unconfirmed) sword he wore drew itself and mowed down the grass, and that it was therefore named "Kusanagi" (草薙).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 40th year of Emperor Keikō, "this year" (是歳)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, 弟橘媛 (reading unconfirmed) is described as a consort (妾), daughter of 忍山宿禰 of the 穗積 (reading unconfirmed) clan, and the storm arises after Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto says, "This is a small sea; I could leap across it." Also, after pacifying the Emishi of Mutsu, he laments three times "吾嬬者耶" (reading unconfirmed) at the 碓日嶺 (reading unconfirmed) pass, longing for 弟橘媛, and in the mountains of Shinano he kills with garlic (蒜) the mountain deity transformed into a white deer.

yamatotakeru-saigo.title: The Death of Yamato Takeru (倭建命) and the White Bird
yamatotakeru-saigo.lead: Returning from the eastern provinces to Owari, Yamato Takeru (倭建命) left the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劔) with Miyazu-hime (美夜受比賣) and set out to seize the mountain deity of Ibuki (伊服岐) bare-handed; he was struck by a great icy rain, kept walking in his weakened body, and died at 能煩野 (reading unconfirmed). Yamato Takeru became an eight-fathom white bird (八尋白智鳥) and flew away; his consorts and children followed it weeping and singing, and the White Bird Tomb (白鳥御陵) was made at 志幾 (reading unconfirmed) in Kawachi.

points.text: Leaving the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劔) with Miyazu-hime (美夜受比賣), Yamato Takeru set out saying he would seize the mountain deity of Ibuki (伊服岐) bare-handed; because he made a declaration (言挙) that a white boar was the deity's messenger, he was struck and confounded by a great icy rain. A small-script note in the original text states that the white boar was in fact the deity itself.

Along the route the weakened Yamato Takeru traveled, the origins of place names such as 居寤清泉, 當藝, 杖衝坂 and 三重 (reading unconfirmed) are told; at 能煩野 (reading unconfirmed) Yamato Takeru composed songs longing for his homeland (思國歌), and when he finished singing he died.

The dead Yamato Takeru became an eight-fathom white bird (八尋白智鳥) and flew away; it is recorded that the four songs his consorts and children composed as they followed it, weeping, are still sung at the great funerals of emperors (大御葬).
The white bird stopped at 志幾 (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Kawachi, and the White Bird Tomb (白鳥御陵) was made there, but the bird flew on from there, soaring through the sky.

In the Nihon Shoki (the 40th year of Emperor Keikō, "this year"), the deity of 膽吹山 (reading unconfirmed) appears as a great serpent, and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (日本武尊) dies at 能褒野 (reading unconfirmed) at the age of thirty. The white bird stops at 琴彈原 in Yamato and at 舊市邑 in Kawachi (reading unconfirmed), and the three tombs were all called White Bird Tombs (白鳥陵).

The Kokugakuin University deity-name database (entry for Ibuki-no-Yama-no-Kami, 伊服岐能山之神) explains that on the question of why Yamato Takeru made a "mistaken" declaration (言挙) there are many arguments, such as theories that take up whether that deity was a target of the subjugation (言向) the emperor had ordered, or the content and spirit of the declaration, and that the debate is not settled.

story.text: Yamato Takeru praised the old man who had continued his song at the 酒折宮 (reading unconfirmed) and gave him the post of governor of the eastern provinces (東國造). Crossing from Kai into Shinano (科野國), he subdued Shinano-no-Saka-no-Kami (科野之坂神), and returning to Owari he went to Miyazu-hime (美夜受比賣), to whom he had earlier made his promise. When Miyazu-hime offered the imperial meal and held up a cup of the imperial sake, there was menstrual blood on the hem of her 意須比 (reading unconfirmed). Yamato Takeru saw it and composed a song, and Miyazu-hime answered with a song.

The two were united, and Yamato Takeru left his sword, the Kusanagi sword (草那藝劔), with Miyazu-hime and set out to seize the mountain deity of Ibuki (伊服岐). Saying, "I will seize the deity of this mountain directly, bare-handed," he climbed the mountain, and at its edge he met a white boar as large as an ox. Yamato Takeru made a declaration (言挙), saying, "This thing that has taken the form of a white boar is the deity's messenger. I will not kill it now; I will kill it on my way back," and climbed on, but a great icy rain fell and struck and confounded him. A small-script note in the original text records that the white boar was not the deity's messenger but the deity itself, and that he was confounded because he had made the declaration.

When he came down the mountain and rested at the clear spring of 玉倉部 (reading unconfirmed), his mind cleared a little, so that spring is called 居寤清泉 (reading unconfirmed). On reaching the 當藝野 (reading unconfirmed) plain he said, "My heart always meant to go soaring through the sky, but now my feet cannot walk and have become 當藝斯玖" (reading unconfirmed), so that place is called 當藝. Going on a little from there he was utterly exhausted and walked slowly leaning on a staff, so that place is called 杖衝坂 (reading unconfirmed). When he reached the single pine at the cape of 尾津 (reading unconfirmed), the sword he had left behind when he ate there before was still there and had not been lost, so Yamato Takeru composed a song.

On reaching the village of 三重 (reading unconfirmed) he said, "My legs feel bent threefold, and I am utterly exhausted," so that place is called 三重. On reaching 能煩野 (reading unconfirmed) he composed a song longing for his homeland, and continued with further songs. The original text calls these songs longing for the homeland (思國歌) and records the one that follows as a half-poem (片歌). When his illness suddenly grew grave, Yamato Takeru composed another song, and as soon as he finished singing it he died.

A fast-horse messenger was sent to the capital, and his consorts and children who were in Yamato came down, made a tomb, and crawled around the 那豆岐田 (reading unconfirmed) fields surrounding it, weeping and singing. Then Yamato Takeru became an eight-fathom white bird (八尋白智鳥), soared through the sky, and flew off toward the shore. His consorts and children followed weeping, forgetting the pain even when their feet were cut on the stubble of bamboo grass, and they composed songs as they waded into the sea and also when the bird alighted on the rocky shore.

These four songs were all sung at Yamato Takeru's funeral, and it is said that to this day they are sung at the great funerals of emperors (大御葬). The white bird flew from that province and stopped at 志幾 (reading unconfirmed) in the province of Kawachi, so a tomb was made there to settle it and was named the White Bird Tomb (白鳥御陵). But the bird flew on from there, soaring through the sky. While Yamato Takeru was going round pacifying the provinces, 七拳脛 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 久米直 (reading unconfirmed), always served him as his cook (膳夫).

Yamato Takeru had six children in all: with 布多遲能伊理毘賣命 (reading unconfirmed) he had 帶中津日子命 (reading unconfirmed), with 弟橘比賣命 (reading unconfirmed) he had 若建王 (reading unconfirmed), and so on. Of these, 帶中津日子命 ruled the realm. 迦具漏比賣命 (reading unconfirmed), granddaughter of 若建王, was taken as wife by Emperor Keikō and bore 大江王 (reading unconfirmed), and 大中比賣命 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 大江王, was the mother of 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed) and Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王). Emperor Keikō died at the age of 137, and his tomb is on the 山邊 (reading unconfirmed) road.

quotes.note: Yamato Takeru's words: "I will seize the deity of this mountain directly, bare-handed."
A small-script note in the original text: the thing that had taken the form of a white boar was not the deity's messenger but the deity itself.
Yamato Takeru became a great white bird, soared through the sky, and flew off toward the shore.
The tomb made at 志幾 (reading unconfirmed) in Kawachi was named the White Bird Tomb (白鳥御陵).

figures.name: The old man who tended the fires (御火燒之老人)
figures.role: Praised for continuing the song at the 酒折宮, he was given the post of governor of the eastern provinces (東國造).

figures.name: Shinano-no-Saka-no-Kami (科野之坂神)
figures.role: The slope deity whom Yamato Takeru subdued after crossing from Kai into Shinano.

figures.name: The Kusanagi sword (草那藝劔)
figures.role: The sword Yamato Takeru left with Miyazu-hime when he headed for the mountain of Ibuki.

figures.name: Ibuki-no-Yama-no-Kami (伊服岐能山之神)
figures.role: The mountain deity who appeared in the form of a white boar as large as an ox and struck and confounded Yamato Takeru with a great icy rain.

figures.name: The eight-fathom white bird (八尋白智鳥)
figures.role: The great white bird into which the dead Yamato Takeru was transformed. It stopped at 志幾 in Kawachi and then flew on.

figures.name: 七拳脛 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Ancestor of the 久米直. He always served Yamato Takeru as his cook while he went round the provinces.

figures.name: 布多遲能伊理毘賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of Emperor 伊玖米 (Emperor Suinin) and consort of Yamato Takeru. She bore 帶中津日子命.

figures.name: 若建王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Yamato Takeru and 弟橘比賣命. His granddaughter 迦具漏比賣命 was taken as wife by Emperor Keikō.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 40th year of Emperor Keikō, "this year" (是歳)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the deity of 膽吹山 (reading unconfirmed) becomes a great serpent and blocks the road, and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto (日本武尊), thinking it was the messenger of the violent deity (荒神), stepped over it and went on. The mountain deity raised clouds and rained down ice, and Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto at last recovered by drinking the water of a spring, so he named that spring 居醒泉 (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 17th year of Emperor Keikō, spring, 3rd month (戊戌朔己酉)
compare.text: Songs with the same words as the songs longing for the homeland (思國歌) that Yamato Takeru composes at 能煩野 (reading unconfirmed) in the Kojiki (such as the song beginning "夜麻登波。久爾能麻本呂婆") are, in the Nihon Shoki, songs that Emperor Keikō composed at 子湯縣 in Hyūga (reading unconfirmed) longing for the capital, and they are called 思邦歌 (songs longing for the homeland).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 7 — the 40th year of Emperor Keikō, "this year" (是歳)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, Yamato Takeru-no-Mikoto dies at 能褒野 (reading unconfirmed) at the age of thirty and is buried in the 能褒野 tomb in Ise Province. He emerged from the tomb as a white bird and flew off toward Yamato, and only his clothes remained in the coffin. The white bird stopped at 琴彈原 in Yamato and at 舊市邑 in Kawachi (reading unconfirmed), and a tomb was made at each; the three tombs were called White Bird Tombs (白鳥陵).

chuai-jingu.title: The Death of Emperor Chūai and the Silla Expedition of 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed)
chuai-jingu.lead: After Emperor Seimu (若帯日子天皇 (reading unconfirmed)) established the provincial governors (国造) and district chiefs (県主), Emperor Chūai (帯中日子天皇 (reading unconfirmed)) refuses to believe a divine oracle and dies suddenly. His chief consort 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed), who followed the oracle, crossed the sea and brought Silla into submission, and after returning to Tsukushi she gave birth to a son (later Emperor Ōjin).

points.text: Emperor Chūai rejected as a "lying deity" the oracle promising to give him a land of treasures in the west, and died on the spot while playing the koto (琴). The deity then announced anew that that land was to be ruled by the child (a boy) in the chief consort's womb.

The deity of the oracle revealed its name: it was the will of Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神), and it was the three great deities 底筒男, 中筒男 and 上筒男 (reading unconfirmed). Having brought Silla into submission, the chief consort enshrined the rough spirit (荒御魂) of the Great Deity of 墨江 (reading unconfirmed) in Silla as a deity to guard the land.

大鞆和気命 (reading unconfirmed) (品陀和気命, later Emperor Ōjin) received this name because at birth he had flesh on his arm like a bracer (鞆). The birth took place after the return from Silla to Tsukushi, and the place where he was born is called 宇美 (reading unconfirmed).

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 8), Emperor Chūai attacks the Kumaso without believing the deity's words, cannot win and returns, and in the 2nd month of his 9th year he suddenly falls ill and dies the next day. It does not say, as the Kojiki does, that he died in the middle of playing the koto.

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 9), after the emperor's death the empress herself becomes the ritual medium (神主) and has Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) play the koto, and the deities name, besides 表筒男, 中筒男 and 底筒男 (reading unconfirmed), the deity dwelling in the 五十鈴宮 (reading unconfirmed) of Ise, Kotoshironushi-no-Kami (事代主神) and others. It does not say, as the Kojiki does, "the will of Amaterasu-Ōmikami."

According to the Kokugakuin University deity-name database, the three deities who revealed their names are 底箇之男命, 中箇之男命 and 上箇之男命 (墨江之三前大神) (reading unconfirmed), who were born in the purification (禊) section of Part 1; they are enshrined at Sumiyoshi Taisha (住吉大社) and have long been worshipped as deities who protect seafaring.

story.text: Emperor Seimu (若帯日子天皇 (reading unconfirmed)) ruled the realm from the 高穴穂宮 of 志賀 (reading unconfirmed) in Ōmi (近淡海). He took as wife 弟財郎女 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 建忍山垂根 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 穂積臣 (reading unconfirmed) and others, and 和訶奴気王 (reading unconfirmed) was born. The emperor made Takeuchi-no-Sukune (建内宿禰) his great minister (大臣), and established the governors (国造) of the large and small provinces, the boundaries between provinces, and the district chiefs (県主) of the large and small districts. The emperor died at the age of 95, and his tomb is at 多他那美 in 沙紀 (reading unconfirmed).

Emperor Chūai (帯中日子天皇 (reading unconfirmed)) ruled the realm from the 豊浦宮 of 穴門 (reading unconfirmed) and the 訶志比宮 of Tsukushi (reading unconfirmed). With 大中津比売命 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 大江王 (reading unconfirmed), he had 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed) and Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王); with his chief consort 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) he had 品夜和気命 and 大鞆和気命 (also named 品陀和気命) (reading unconfirmed). The name 大鞆和気命 comes from the fact that at birth he had flesh on his arm like a bracer (鞆). The Kojiki records that from this it is known that he was destined to rule the land from the time he was in his mother's womb. In this reign the 屯家 of 淡道 (reading unconfirmed) was established.

The chief consort 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was a person through whom deities spoke. When the emperor, at the 訶志比宮 (reading unconfirmed), was about to attack the land of 熊曾 (reading unconfirmed), the emperor played the koto, and the great minister Takeuchi-no-Sukune (建内宿禰), in the ritual ground (沙庭), sought the words of the deity. The deity who possessed the chief consort announced, "In the west there is a land with many dazzling treasures, gold and silver first among them. I will give you that land." The emperor answered, "When I climb a high place and look west, I see no land, only the great sea," and, declaring it a deity that spoke lies, pushed the koto away, stopped playing and fell silent. The deity was greatly angered and said, "This realm is not a land for you to rule. Head for the one road (一道)."

Urged by Takeuchi-no-Sukune, the emperor drew the koto a little closer and began to play, but soon the sound of the koto could no longer be heard. When they lit a light and looked, the emperor was already dead. In fear, the people placed the emperor in a temporary mortuary palace (殯宮), gathered great offerings (大奴佐) from throughout the land, sought out every kind of offense, and performed a great purification (大祓) of the land. When Takeuchi-no-Sukune again sought the words of the deity, the deity announced as before that this land was to be ruled by the child in the chief consort's womb, and answered that the child was a boy. When asked its name, the deity revealed that this was the will of Amaterasu-Ōmikami (天照大神), and also that it was the three great deities 底筒男, 中筒男 and 上筒男 (reading unconfirmed).

The deity instructed them to make offerings (幣帛) to all the heavenly and earthly deities and to the deities of the mountains, rivers and seas, to enshrine its own spirit on the ships, to put the ash of 真木 (reading unconfirmed) wood into gourds, and to make many chopsticks and 比羅伝 (reading unconfirmed), scatter them floating on the sea, and so cross. When they arrayed the army and lined up the ships as instructed and crossed, the fish of the sea, large and small alike, bore the ships on their backs, a strong following wind blew, and the waves carried the ships halfway into the land of Silla. The king of Silla, in awe, offered that from then on he would serve as the emperor's horse-keepers (御馬甘), sending ships in a row every year without rest. Thus the land of Silla was designated as the horse-keepers and the land of Paekche as the 屯家 across the sea (渡屯家) (reading unconfirmed); the chief consort thrust her staff into the gate of the ruler of Silla, enshrined the rough spirit (荒御魂) of the Great Deity of 墨江 (reading unconfirmed) as a deity to guard the land, and returned.

Before that work was finished, the chief consort reached the month of her delivery, so to calm her womb she took stones and wound them around the waist of her skirt, and she gave birth to the child after crossing to Tsukushi. Therefore the place where the child was born is called 宇美 (reading unconfirmed), and the stones she wound in her skirt are in the village of 伊斗 (reading unconfirmed) in Tsukushi. Also, the chief consort took a meal on the riverbank at the village of 玉嶋 in the district of 末羅 (reading unconfirmed) in the first ten days of the 4th month; she sat on a rock in the river, pulled out threads from her skirt, used grains of rice as bait, and fished for the sweetfish (年魚) of that river. The text records that for this reason, even now, in the first ten days of the 4th month women never fail to pull threads from their skirts and fish for sweetfish with grains of rice as bait.

quotes.note: In the west there is a land. Many treasures of all kinds, gold and silver first among them, so dazzling they blind the eyes, are in that land (words the deity announced through the mouth of the chief consort).
This land is a land to be ruled by the child in your (the chief consort's) womb (words the deity announced again after the emperor's death).
Because he had flesh on his arm like a bracer (鞆), that name (大鞆和気命 (reading unconfirmed)) was given.
The fish of the sea, large and small alike, all bore the ships on their backs across.

figures.name: 若帶日子天皇 (reading unconfirmed) (Emperor Seimu)
figures.role: Emperor Seimu. He made Takeuchi-no-Sukune his great minister and established the provincial governors, provincial boundaries and district chiefs.

figures.name: 大中津比賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of 大江王. With Emperor Chūai she bore 香坂王 and Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王).

figures.name: 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor Chūai and 大中津比売命, and elder brother of Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王).

figures.name: 品夜和氣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor Chūai and 息長帯比売命, and elder brother of 大鞆和気命.

figures.name: The koto (御琴)
figures.role: The koto the emperor played to seek the words of the deity. His pushing it away and ceasing to play brought on the deity's anger.

figures.name: The ruler of Silla (新羅國主)
figures.role: In awe at the ships surging into his land, he swore to serve as horse-keepers (御馬甘), and the chief consort's staff was thrust into his gate.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 8 — the 9th year of Emperor Chūai, spring, 2nd month (癸卯朔丁未)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, Emperor Chūai, not believing the words of the deity, attacks the Kumaso, cannot win and returns, then suddenly falls ill and dies the next day; it records that he died early because he did not heed the deity's words. An alternative account (一云) in a small-script note gives another tradition, that he attacked the Kumaso and died after being hit by an enemy arrow.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9 — Empress Jingū (the 9th year of Emperor Chūai, 3rd month, 壬申朔)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, after the emperor's death the empress chooses an auspicious day, enters a ritual palace (斎宮), becomes the ritual medium (神主) herself, has Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) play the koto, and has 中臣烏賊津使主 (reading unconfirmed) act as the interpreter of the divine words (審神者) to ask the names of the deities. In the Kojiki it is the emperor who plays the koto, and Takeuchi-no-Sukune is in the ritual ground (沙庭).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9 — Empress Jingū (the 9th year of Emperor Chūai, summer, 4th month, 壬寅朔甲辰)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, fishing in the stream at the village of 玉嶋 (reading unconfirmed) using thread from her skirt as a fishing line takes place before the crossing to Silla, as a divination of whether her wish to obtain the land of treasures in the west would be fulfilled, and it is given as the origin of calling that place the land of 梅豆羅 (now 松浦) (reading unconfirmed). In the Kojiki, it is placed as a story after the birth of the child.

oshikuma.title: The Rebellion of Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王) and Kehi-no-Ōkami (気比大神)
oshikuma.lead: Returning from Silla, 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) went up to Yamato in a mourning ship, pretending that her son had died, and defeated the brothers 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed) and Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王), who lay in wait for her. Afterwards, when Takeuchi-no-Sukune (建内宿禰) took the prince to 角鹿 (reading unconfirmed), Izasawake-no-Ōkami-no-Mikoto (伊奢沙和気大神之命) asked to exchange names, and from this arose the name Miketsu-Ōkami (御食津大神; Kehi-no-Ōkami, 気比大神); when the prince returned to the capital, his mother welcomed him with sake and song.

points.text: 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) put her son on a mourning ship (喪船) and made it appear that he had died, deceiving 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed) and Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王), who lay in wait. 香坂王 was devoured by an enraged boar in the middle of an oath-hunt (宇気比獦), and Oshikuma-no-Miko, defeated, entered the sea with 伊佐比宿禰 (reading unconfirmed) and died.

What decided the outcome was the stratagem of 建振熊命 (reading unconfirmed), the general on the crown prince's side. He had it announced that "息長帯日売命 has died" and made a show of cutting his bowstrings, and after the enemy had put away their weapons, he strung the spare strings he had hidden in his hair and attacked.

At 角鹿 (reading unconfirmed), Izasawake-no-Ōkami-no-Mikoto (伊奢沙和気大神之命) asked to exchange names with the crown prince and drove 入鹿魚 (reading unconfirmed) fish onto the shore. Because the crown prince said, "You have given me fish for my meal (御食)," the name Miketsu-Ōkami (御食津大神) arose, and by the time the Kojiki was written the deity was called Kehi-no-Ōkami (気比大神). The place names 血浦 and 都奴賀 (reading unconfirmed) are also explained from this story.

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 9), it is a red boar that appears in a divination hunt (祈狩) at 菟餓野 (reading unconfirmed) that devours 麛坂王 (香坂王) (reading unconfirmed), and the stratagem of hiding bowstrings in the hair and proposing a false peace is carried out by Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰). Oshikuma-no-Miko sinks at the 瀬田 (reading unconfirmed) crossing together with 五十狭茅宿禰 (reading unconfirmed) and dies.

In the Nihon Shoki, the crown prince worships the Great Deity 笥飯大神 (reading unconfirmed) of 角鹿 in the 2nd month of the 13th year of the regency (摂政), and the story of the exchange of names appears as an alternative account (一云) in a small-script note at the beginning of the book of Emperor Ōjin (Book 10); while it says the Great Deity is called 去来紗別神 and the crown prince 誉田別尊 (reading unconfirmed), it states that there is no record of the original names and that they are "unknown" (未詳).

According to the Kokugakuin University deity-name database, the "須久那美迦微" (reading unconfirmed) appearing in the mother's song is regarded as another name of Sukunahikona-no-Kami (少名毘古那神), and here it is praised as a deity of sake. Also, because the Kojiki does not say what happened as a result of the exchange of names, theories are divided on the meaning of the exchange.

story.text: When 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was returning to Yamato, she distrusted the people's loyalty, so she prepared a mourning ship (喪船), put her son on it, and had it spread about that the prince had already died. Hearing this, 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed) and Oshikuma-no-Miko (忍熊王) planned to lie in wait and strike, and went out to 斗賀野 (reading unconfirmed) and held an oath-hunt (宇気比獦). While 香坂王 was up in an 歴木 (reading unconfirmed) tree, a great enraged boar came out, dug the tree down, and devoured 香坂王.

His younger brother Oshikuma-no-Miko, unafraid of this, raised an army and lay in wait, intending to attack the mourning ship as if it were empty. Then soldiers came down from the mourning ship and battle began. On Oshikuma-no-Miko's side, 伊佐比宿禰 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 難波吉師部 (reading unconfirmed), was general; on the crown prince's side, 難波根子建振熊命 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 丸邇臣 (reading unconfirmed), was general. Oshikuma-no-Miko's army was driven back as far as 山代 (reading unconfirmed), but there it turned to face them, and neither army retreated as they fought.

建振熊命 (reading unconfirmed) devised a stratagem: he had it announced, "息長帯日売命 has already died, so there is no further reason to fight," and cut his bowstrings to make it look as if he had surrendered. The opposing general believed this, unstrung his bows and put away his weapons. Then 建振熊命's side took out the spare strings (also called 宇佐由豆留 (reading unconfirmed)) they had hidden in their hair, restrung their bows, and pursued and attacked. Oshikuma-no-Miko's army fled to 逢坂 (reading unconfirmed) and fought again, but was cut down to the last man at 沙沙那美 (reading unconfirmed).
Driven to the end, Oshikuma-no-Miko and 伊佐比宿禰 (reading unconfirmed) boarded a boat, floated out on the sea, and sang a song. Then they entered the sea together and died.

Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto (建内宿禰命) took the crown prince to perform purification (禊), went round the lands of Ōmi (淡海) and Wakasa (若狭), built a temporary palace at 角鹿 in 高志前 (reading unconfirmed), and stayed there. That night, Izasawake-no-Ōkami-no-Mikoto (伊奢沙和気大神之命), who dwells in that place, appeared in a dream and said, "I wish to exchange my name for the prince's name." When they reverently agreed, the deity announced, "Tomorrow morning go out to the shore. I will make a gift as a sign of the exchange of names." The next morning, when they went out to the shore, 入鹿魚 (reading unconfirmed) fish with wounded noses filled an entire bay.

The prince had it said to the deity, "You have given me fish for my meal (御食)." Therefore the deity's name was praised and he was called Miketsu-Ōkami (御食津大神), and he is now called Kehi-no-Ōkami (気比大神). Also, because the blood from the noses of the 入鹿魚 smelled, that bay was named 血浦, and it is now called 都奴賀 (reading unconfirmed), the text records.

When the prince returned to the capital, his mother 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) brewed waiting-sake (待酒) and presented it, singing a song as she offered the great sake. Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto sang an answering song on the prince's behalf, and the text records that these are songs of sake-revelry (酒楽歌). Finally it concludes that Emperor Chūai (帯中津日子天皇 (reading unconfirmed)) died at the age of 52, and that his tomb is at 長江 in 恵賀 in Kawachi (reading unconfirmed).

quotes.note: A great enraged boar came out, dug down that 歴木 (reading unconfirmed) tree, and devoured 香坂王.
He had it announced, "息長帯日売命 has already died, so there is no further need to fight," and made a show of cutting his bowstrings (the stratagem of 建振熊命 (reading unconfirmed)).
"You have given me fish for my meal (御食)." Therefore the deity's name was praised and he was called Miketsu-Ōkami (御食津大神).
These are songs of sake-revelry (酒楽歌) (the name collectively given to the song of 息長帯日売命 (reading unconfirmed) and the answering song of Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto).

figures.name: 香坂王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Elder brother of Oshikuma-no-Miko. He was devoured by an enraged boar in the middle of an oath-hunt (宇気比獦).

figures.name: 伊佐比宿禰 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: General on Oshikuma-no-Miko's side (ancestor of the 難波吉師部). In the end he entered the sea with Oshikuma-no-Miko and died.

figures.name: 難波根子建振熊命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: General on the crown prince's side (ancestor of the 丸邇臣). With a false surrender he got the enemy to put away their weapons and defeated Oshikuma-no-Miko's army.

figures.name: The mourning ship (喪船)
figures.role: The ship on which the prince was placed to make it appear that he had died. Oshikuma-no-Miko tried to attack this ship.

figures.name: Miketsu-Ōkami (御食津大神)
figures.role: A name given in praise of Izasawake-no-Ōkami-no-Mikoto (伊奢沙和気大神之命) because he gave the crown prince fish (入鹿魚) for his meal (御食).

figures.name: Kehi-no-Ōkami (氣比大神)
figures.role: The name by which Izasawake-no-Ōkami-no-Mikoto (伊奢沙和気大神之命), who dwells at 角鹿, was called at the time the Kojiki was written.

figures.name: 入鹿魚 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The fish with wounded noses driven onto the shore as a sign of the exchange of names. The name 血浦 came from the smell of the blood from their noses.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9 — Empress Jingū (spring, 2nd month of the year after the attack on Silla)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, 麛坂王 (reading unconfirmed) and Oshikuma-no-Miko gathered soldiers under the pretense of building the emperor's tomb, and when they held a divination hunt (祈狩) at 菟餓野 (reading unconfirmed), a red boar climbed onto the temporary viewing stand and devoured 麛坂王. The empress does not use a mourning ship; she has Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) hold the prince in his arms and go round by the southern sea to the 水門 of Kii (紀伊水門).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9 — Empress Jingū (entries from the 3rd month, 丙申朔庚子)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, it is Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) who has the whole army hide spare bowstrings in their hair, falsely proposes peace, and gets Oshikuma-no-Miko's army to cut their bowstrings and throw their weapons into the river (in the Kojiki it is 建振熊命 (reading unconfirmed)).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 9 — the 13th year of the regency of Empress Jingū, spring, 2nd month (丁巳朔甲子)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) takes the crown prince to worship the Great Deity 笥飯大神 (reading unconfirmed) of 角鹿, and when the crown prince returns, the empress dowager (皇太后) entertains him at a banquet and sings, and Takeuchi-no-Sukune sings a reply on the crown prince's behalf. The stories of the exchange of names and of the 入鹿魚 are not in this entry.

ojin-tsumadoi.title: Emperor Ōjin's Courtships and 髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed)
ojin-tsumadoi.lead: 品陀和気命 (reading unconfirmed) (Emperor Ōjin) asked 大山守命 and 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) which they found dearer, an elder child or a younger child, and designated 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) as his successor. The emperor was united with 宮主矢河枝比売 (reading unconfirmed) at the village of 木幡 (reading unconfirmed); 髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed), whom he had summoned from Hyūga, was given to 大雀命 at 大雀命's request; and the 国主 of Yoshino (吉野之國主 (reading unconfirmed)) presented sake and songs.

points.text: Emperor Ōjin asked 大山守命 and 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) which was dearer, an elder child or a younger child, and approved the words of 大雀命, who, grasping the emperor's mind, answered "the younger child." As a result it was decided that 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) would be the one to inherit the heavenly succession (天津日継), 大山守命 the one to take charge of the government of the mountains and seas, and 大雀命 the one to take charge of the government of the realm (食国).

The mother of 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) is 宮主矢河枝比売 (reading unconfirmed) (daughter of 比布礼能意富美 of 丸邇 (reading unconfirmed)), whom the emperor met at a fork in the road in the village of 木幡 (reading unconfirmed). The next day the emperor was entertained at her house, accepted a cup, and sang a long song.

髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed), who had been summoned from Hyūga, was given by the emperor to 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed), because 大雀命, who had been charmed by her at the port of Naniwa (難波津), made a request through Takeuchi-no-Sukune (建内宿禰). At the 豊明 (reading unconfirmed) banquet the emperor had 髪長比売 hold the oak-leaf cup (柏) of great sake and hand it over.

The text records a song by the 国主 of Yoshino (reading unconfirmed) praising 大雀命's sword, and a song they sing while presenting sake brewed in a 横臼 (reading unconfirmed) mortar and drumming with their mouths (口鼓); the latter is said to be the song the 国主 still sing whenever they present great tribute offerings (大贄).

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 10), the exchange about the elder child and the younger child takes place in the 1st month of the 40th year of Emperor Ōjin, and on the 甲子 day of the same month 菟道稚郎子 (reading unconfirmed) is made successor, 大山守命 is entrusted with the mountains, rivers, forests and fields, and 大鷦鷯尊 (reading unconfirmed) with assisting the crown prince. The Kojiki gives no year and places it directly after the emperor's genealogy.

In the Nihon Shoki, the emperor himself notices the love of 大鷦鷯尊 (reading unconfirmed) and gives him 髪長媛 (reading unconfirmed), and Takeuchi-no-Sukune's mediation is not written. The story of meeting 宮主矢河枝比売 at the village of 木幡 could not be confirmed in Book 10; only the fact that 宮主宅媛 (reading unconfirmed) became a consort and bore 菟道稚郎子 and others appears.

story.text: 品陀和気命 (reading unconfirmed) (Emperor Ōjin) ruled the realm from the 明宮 of 軽嶋 (reading unconfirmed). He took many wives, beginning with three princesses, daughters of 品陀真若王: 高木之入日売命, 中日売命 and 弟日売命 (reading unconfirmed). The text records that his children numbered twenty-six in all (eleven princes and fifteen princesses), and that among them 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) ruled the realm.

The emperor wished to have 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) rule the realm, and asked 大山守命 and 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed), "Which is dearer, an elder child or a younger child?" 大山守命 answered the elder child. 大雀命, perceiving the emperor's mind, answered, "The elder child is already grown, so there is no need to worry about him, but the younger child is not yet grown, so he is dearer." The emperor said, "The words of 佐邪岐阿芸 (reading unconfirmed) are just as I think," and ordered 大山守命 to administer the government of the mountains and seas and 大雀命 to administer the government of the realm (食国) and report to the emperor, and decided that 宇遅能和紀郎子 would inherit the heavenly succession (天津日継). 大雀命 did not go against the emperor's command.

Once, when the emperor went out to the province of Ōmi (近淡海国), he stood on the 宇遅野 plain, looked out toward 葛野 (reading unconfirmed), and sang a song. On reaching the village of 木幡 (reading unconfirmed), he met a beautiful girl at a fork in the road. When he asked her name, she answered that she was 宮主矢河枝比売 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 比布礼能意富美 of 丸邇 (reading unconfirmed), so the emperor told her, "Tomorrow, on my way back, I will stop at your house." Her father, knowing he was the emperor and in awe, decorated the house and waited. At the reception the next day, when 矢河枝比売 offered a cup of great sake, the emperor sang a long song while having her hold the cup.

The child born of this union was 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed). The emperor heard of 髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of the 諸県君 (reading unconfirmed) of the province of Hyūga, whose looks were beautiful, and sent a messenger to summon her. The crown prince 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) saw 髪長比売 when she arrived at the port of Naniwa (難波津), was moved by her appearance, and asked the great minister Takeuchi-no-Sukune (建内宿禰大臣) to request that the emperor grant her to him. On the day of the 豊明 (reading unconfirmed) banquet the emperor had 髪長比売 hold the oak-leaf cup (柏) of great sake, gave her to the crown prince, and sang a song.
The emperor sang one more song and gave 髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed) to him. After receiving 髪長比売, the crown prince also sang two songs.

Also, the 国主 of Yoshino (吉野之國主 (reading unconfirmed)), seeing the sword 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) was wearing, sang a song. They made a 横臼 (reading unconfirmed) mortar above the 白檮 oaks of Yoshino, and when they brewed great sake in that mortar and presented it, they sang a song while drumming with their mouths (口鼓) and performing gestures. The text records that this song is the one the 国主 have always sung, down to the present, every time they present great tribute offerings (大贄).

quotes.note: The elder child is already grown, so there is no need to worry. The younger child is not yet grown, so he is dear (the answer of 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed)).
宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) shall inherit the heavenly succession (天津日継) (one of the divisions of roles the emperor decided).
He had 髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed) hold the oak-leaf cup (柏) of great sake and gave her to the crown prince (大雀命).
It is the song the 国主 have always sung, down to the present, every time they present great tribute offerings (大贄).

figures.name: 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor Ōjin. Entrusted with the government of the realm (食国) for an answer that grasped the emperor's mind, he was granted 髪長比売. He later rules the realm.

figures.name: 宇遲能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor Ōjin and 宮主矢河枝比売. The emperor designated him as the one to inherit the heavenly succession (天津日継).

figures.name: 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor Ōjin. He answered the question with "the elder child" and was entrusted with the government of the mountains and seas.

figures.name: 宮主矢河枝比賣 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of 比布礼能意富美 of 丸邇. She met the emperor at the village of 木幡 and bore 宇遅能和紀郎子.

figures.name: 髮長比賣 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of the 諸県君 of the province of Hyūga. Summoned by the emperor, she was given to 大雀命 at his request.

figures.name: 品陀眞若王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Father of the three princesses 高木之入日売命, 中日売命 and 弟日売命.

figures.name: The 国主 of Yoshino (吉野之國主) (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: People of Yoshino. They sang a song praising 大雀命's sword and a song for presenting sake.

figures.name: The oak-leaf cup of great sake (大御酒柏)
figures.role: The sake vessel that, on the day of the 豊明 banquet, the emperor had 髪長比売 hold and hand to the crown prince.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10 — the 40th year of Emperor Ōjin, spring, 1st month (辛丑朔戊申)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the emperor asks 大山守命 and 大鷦鷯尊 (reading unconfirmed), "Do you hold your children dear?" and then asks which, the elder or the younger. The emperor is displeased by 大山守命's answer and delighted by 大鷦鷯尊's answer. It differs from the Kojiki in that the year and month are recorded.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10 — the 13th year of Emperor Ōjin, autumn, 9th month
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the emperor, who had heard of the reputation of 髪長媛 (reading unconfirmed) in the 11th year, sent a messenger to summon her in the 3rd month of the 13th year, and she arrived in the 9th month and was lodged at 桑津邑 (reading unconfirmed). The emperor learns of 大鷦鷯尊's love and, at a banquet in the inner palace, points to 髪長媛 and sings a song, giving her to him.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10 — the 19th year of Emperor Ōjin, winter, 10th month (戊戌朔)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, when the emperor went to the Yoshino palace (吉野宮), the 国樔 (reading unconfirmed) people presented sweet sake (醴酒) and sang, and when they finished singing they struck their mouths, looked up and laughed; it records that even now the 国樔 do the same on the day they present local products (土毛). This corresponds to the "吉野之国主等" (the 国主 of Yoshino) of the Kojiki.

ojin-oyamamori.title: The Age of Emperor Ōjin and the Rebellion of 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed)
ojin-oyamamori.lead: In the reign of Emperor Ōjin, groups such as the 海部 and 山部 (reading unconfirmed) were established, and from Paekche came horses, a sword and a great mirror, 和邇吉師 (reading unconfirmed) bearing the Analects (論語) and the Thousand Character Classic (千字文), and people skilled in smithing, weaving and sake-brewing. After the emperor's death, 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed) tried to kill his younger brother 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) and seize the realm, but he fell into a trap and sank in the river; later 宇遅能和紀郎子 also died young, and 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) ruled the realm.

points.text: When Emperor Ōjin died, 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed) defied his father's command, aimed at the realm, and tried to kill his younger brother 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed). 宇遅能和紀郎子, who had prepared after being warned by 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed), disguised himself as the boatman at the steering oar, tipped the boat, and made 大山守命 fall into the river and sink.

大雀命 and 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) each yielded the realm to the other, and meanwhile the fishermen (海人) carrying the great tribute offerings (大贄) wept, worn out from going back and forth. Because 宇遅能和紀郎子 died young, 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) came to rule the realm.

The text records that from Paekche came 阿知吉師 (reading unconfirmed) with horses and 和邇吉師 (reading unconfirmed) with ten scrolls of the Analects (論語) and one scroll of the Thousand Character Classic (千字文), as well as the smith 卓素, the 呉服 西素 (reading unconfirmed), the ancestors of the 秦造 and the 漢直 (reading unconfirmed), and 須須許理 (reading unconfirmed), who brewed sake.

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 10), sea people (海人) and mountain wardens (山守部) were established in the provinces in the 8th month of the 5th year; in the 9th month of the 7th year Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) led the 韓人 who had come to court in making a pond, which was named the 韓人池 (reading unconfirmed); and in the 10th month of the 11th year the 剣池, 軽池, 鹿垣池 and 廐坂池 (reading unconfirmed) ponds were made. In the Kojiki, the pond made using people of Silla is the Paekche Pond (百済池).

In the Nihon Shoki, in the 8th month of the 15th year the king of Paekche had 阿直岐 (reading unconfirmed) present two fine horses, and on 阿直岐's recommendation 王仁 (reading unconfirmed) came in the 2nd month of the 16th year and became the teacher of the crown prince 菟道稚郎子 (reading unconfirmed). The titles of the Analects and the Thousand Character Classic found in the Kojiki do not appear in this Nihon Shoki entry.

For the rebellion of 大山守命 and the story of 大雀命 and 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) yielding the realm to each other, no corresponding entry could be confirmed in the book of Emperor Ōjin (Book 10). Book 10 ends with the emperor's death in the 2nd month of the 41st year and the entries of that month.

story.text: In this reign the groups 海部, 山部, 山守部 and 伊勢部 (reading unconfirmed) were established, and the 剣池 (reading unconfirmed) pond was made. Because people of Silla came over, Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto (建内宿禰命) led them, assigned them to the work of building embankments and ponds, and made the Paekche Pond (百済池). 照古王 (reading unconfirmed), ruler of Paekche, presented one stallion and one mare, sending them with 阿知吉師 (reading unconfirmed), and also presented a sword and a great mirror. When the emperor ordered Paekche, "If there is a wise man, present him," a man named 和邇吉師 (reading unconfirmed) came bearing ten scrolls of the Analects (論語) and one scroll of the Thousand Character Classic (千字文), eleven scrolls in all (a note says 和邇吉師 is the ancestor of the 文首 (reading unconfirmed) and others).

In addition there came the craftsman 卓素 (reading unconfirmed), a 韓鍛 smith; the 呉服 西素, two people (reading unconfirmed); the ancestor of the 秦造; the ancestor of the 漢直 (reading unconfirmed); and 仁番 (also named 須須許理) (reading unconfirmed), who knew how to brew sake. The emperor enjoyed the great sake brewed by 須須許理 and sang a song. When he went out just as he was, the emperor struck a large stone on the 大坂 (reading unconfirmed) road with his staff, and the stone ran away, and so the proverb "Even a hard stone avoids a drunkard" arose.

After the emperor died, 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) yielded the realm to 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) in accordance with the emperor's command. But 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed) defied the emperor's command and, wishing to take the realm, secretly prepared troops intending to kill his younger brother. When 大雀命 heard of this, he sent a messenger to inform 宇遅能和紀郎子. 宇遅能和紀郎子 hid troops by the river, put up a fence and curtains on the hilltop, seated an attendant (舎人) disguised as the prince on a seat (呉床), and had officials come and go respectfully, arranging it to look like the place where the prince was.

宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) decorated the boat his elder brother would use to cross the river, and smeared the juice obtained by pounding the roots of 佐那葛 (reading unconfirmed) on the 簀椅 (reading unconfirmed) inside the boat so that anyone stepping on it would fall. He himself put on a cloth robe and trousers (褌), took on the appearance of a lowly person, took the steering oar and stood in the boat. 大山守命, who had come to the riverbank wearing armor under his clothes, assumed that the one sitting in the decorated place was his younger brother and, not realizing that the man at the oar was his brother, asked, "I hear there is an angry great boar on this mountain. I wish to take that boar; will I be able to?" The man at the oar answered, "You will not be able to take it, because it has been tried many times and it could not be taken," and tipped the boat in the middle of the river, so 大山守命 fell into the water and, floating and being carried along, sang a song.

The troops hidden by the river rose up all at once from both banks and aimed their arrows at him, so 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed) was carried along and sank at the cape of 訶和羅 (reading unconfirmed). When they searched where he had sunk with hooks, the hooks caught on the armor inside his clothes and it rang "訶和羅," so that place is called 訶和羅前. When the bones were pulled up, his younger brother, the prince, sang a song. The bones of 大山守命 were buried on 那良山 (reading unconfirmed), and 大山守命 is regarded as the ancestor of the 土形君, 弊岐君 and 榛原君 (reading unconfirmed) and others.

After that, 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed) and 宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed) each yielded the realm to the other. Meanwhile, when fishermen (海人) came to present the great tribute offerings (大贄), the elder brother declined and had them present them to the younger, and the younger declined and had them present them to the elder, so that, as many days passed, the fishermen wept, worn out from going back and forth. So arose the proverb "The fishermen weep because of their own goods." However, 宇遅能和紀郎子 died young, so 大雀命 ruled the realm.

quotes.note: Ten scrolls of the Analects (論語) and one scroll of the Thousand Character Classic (千字文), eleven scrolls in all (the books brought by 和邇吉師 (reading unconfirmed)).
So there is the proverb, "Even a hard stone avoids a drunkard."
That prince (宇遅能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed)) put on a cloth robe and trousers (褌), took on the appearance of a lowly person, took the steering oar and stood in the boat.
So there is the proverb, "The fishermen weep because of their own goods."

figures.name: 大山守命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor Ōjin. He defied his father's command and aimed at the realm, and sank in the river through his younger brother's stratagem.

figures.name: 宇遲能和紀郎子 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The younger prince to whom the realm was yielded. Disguised as the boatman at the oar, he struck down 大山守命, but later died young.

figures.name: 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: He informed his younger brother of their elder brother's plot, and after the two yielded the realm to each other, he ruled the realm.

figures.name: 照古王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Ruler of Paekche. He presented two horses, a sword and a great mirror.

figures.name: 阿知吉師 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The man sent with the horses presented by 照古王 (a note says he is the ancestor of the 阿直史 and others).

figures.name: 和邇吉師 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The man who brought the Analects and the Thousand Character Classic from Paekche (a note says he is the ancestor of the 文首 and others).

figures.name: 須須許理 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A man from overseas who knew how to brew sake (also named 仁番). He presented the great sake he brewed to the emperor.

figures.name: 佐那葛 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The juice obtained by pounding its roots was smeared on the 簀椅 of the boat so that 大山守命 would fall if he stepped on it.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10 — the 5th year of Emperor Ōjin, autumn, 8th month (庚寅朔壬寅)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, sea people (海人) and mountain wardens (山守部) were established in the provinces. The Kojiki lists four: the 海部, 山部, 山守部 and 伊勢部 (reading unconfirmed).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10 — the 7th year of Emperor Ōjin, autumn, 9th month
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, Takeuchi-no-Sukune (武内宿禰) led the 韓人 who had come to court in making a pond, and named it the 韓人池 (reading unconfirmed). In the Kojiki, the pond that Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto made using people of Silla is the Paekche Pond (百済池).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 10 — the 15th year of Emperor Ōjin, autumn, 8th month (壬戌朔丁卯)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the king of Paekche had 阿直岐 (reading unconfirmed) present two fine horses, which were kept in the stable at 軽坂上 (reading unconfirmed). Because 阿直岐 could read the classics, he became the teacher of the crown prince 菟道稚郎子 (reading unconfirmed), and he further recommended 王仁 (reading unconfirmed) as an excellent scholar. In the Kojiki, the one who brought the horses is 阿知吉師 (reading unconfirmed), and the seeking of a capable man is done at the emperor's command.

amenohiboko.title: Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛) and the Brothers of Autumn Mountain and Spring Mountain
amenohiboko.lead: Long ago, Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛), son of the ruler of Silla, crossed over to Japan in pursuit of his wife, who had been born from a red jewel; he settled in 多遅摩 (reading unconfirmed), and from his descendants came the mother of 息長帯比売命 (reading unconfirmed). The eight treasures Ame-no-Hiboko brought are regarded as Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami (伊豆志之八前大神), and over that deity's daughter, Izushi-otome-no-Kami (伊豆志袁登売神), the brothers Akiyama-no-Shitahi-otoko (秋山之下氷壮夫) and Haruyama-no-Kasumi-otoko (春山之霞壮夫) made a wager; the elder brother, who broke his promise, suffered for eight years under his mother's curse.

points.text: Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛) was the son of the ruler of Silla. He crossed over in pursuit of his wife, who had been born from a red jewel borne by a woman touched by the light of the sun, and who had fled to Naniwa. But he was blocked by the deity of the crossing and could not enter Naniwa, so he stayed in the province of 多遅摩 (reading unconfirmed).

Between 多遅摩比多訶 and 由良度美 (reading unconfirmed), descendants of Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛), was born 葛城之高額比売命 (reading unconfirmed), and her child is 息長帯比売命 (reading unconfirmed) (Empress Jingū). In the Kojiki, 息長帯比売命, who crossed over to Silla, is regarded as a descendant of Ame-no-Hiboko.

A note states that the eight treasures brought by Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛) (two strings of beads, four kinds of scarves (比礼) and the 奥津鏡 and 辺津鏡 mirrors (reading unconfirmed)) are Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami (伊豆志之八前大神).

Haruyama-no-Kasumi-otoko (春山之霞壮夫) was united with Izushi-otome-no-Kami (伊豆志袁登売神) by means of the wisteria clothes and the bow and arrows his mother made; his elder brother Akiyama-no-Shitahi-otoko (秋山之下氷壮夫), who did not pay the stakes of the wager, fell ill for eight years under his mother's curse, and only after weeping and apologizing was he restored.

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 6), the arrival of Ame-no-Hiboko (天日槍) takes place in the 3rd month of the 3rd year of Emperor Suinin, and the treasures are seven kinds, 羽太玉, 足高玉, 鵜鹿鹿赤石玉, 出石小刀, 出石桙, 日鏡 and 熊神籬 (reading unconfirmed), which were deposited in Tajima Province. In the genealogy of an alternative account (一云) in a small-script note, 清彦 (reading unconfirmed) is the father of 田道間守 (reading unconfirmed), which differs from the Kojiki, where 清日子 and 多遅麻毛理 (reading unconfirmed) are brothers.

According to the Kokugakuin University deity-name database, the story of the autumn-mountain and spring-mountain brothers is found only in the Kojiki. It has many points in common with the story of 海幸 and 山幸 (reading unconfirmed) at the end of Part 1, such as the younger brother defeating the elder, the use of bamboo work, and submission brought about by the ebb and flow of the tide, and the theory that the two were deliberately placed at the ends of Part 1 and Part 2 is regarded as influential.

story.text: Long ago, a man named Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛), son of the ruler of Silla, crossed over to Japan. The reason was this. Beside a marsh called 阿具奴摩 (reading unconfirmed) in Silla, a lowly woman was taking a midday nap when the light of the sun shone like a rainbow on her private parts. A lowly man who found this strange kept constant watch over the woman. From the time of that nap the woman became pregnant and gave birth to a red jewel. The man obtained the jewel and always kept it wrapped and tied at his waist.

Because the man had fields in a valley, he loaded an ox with food for the people working in the fields and went into the valley, where he met Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛). Ame-no-Hiboko said, "You mean to kill this ox and eat it," and seized the man, intending to put him in prison. The man answered that he was only carrying food for the people in the fields, but he was not released; he offered Ame-no-Hiboko the jewel from his waist and was released. When Ame-no-Hiboko placed the jewel beside his bed, it became a beautiful maiden, so he made her his chief wife.

His wife always prepared all kinds of fine dishes for her husband to eat, but Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛) grew arrogant and reviled her. His wife said, "I am not a woman who should be your wife. I will go to the land of my ancestors," and secretly boarded a small boat, fled across, and stayed at Naniwa (a note says she is Akaru-hime-no-Kami (阿加流比売神), who dwells at the 比売碁曽社 (reading unconfirmed) shrine in Naniwa). When Ame-no-Hiboko heard that his wife had fled, he crossed over in pursuit, but as he was about to reach Naniwa, the deity of the crossing blocked the way and would not let him in. So he turned back, anchored in the province of 多遅摩 (reading unconfirmed), and stayed there.

Ame-no-Hiboko (天之日矛) married 前津見 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 多遅摩之俣尾 (reading unconfirmed), and his descendants continued through 多遅摩母呂須玖, 多遅摩斐泥 and 多遅摩比那良岐 (reading unconfirmed), whose children were the three 多遅麻毛理, 多遅摩比多訶 and 清日子 (reading unconfirmed). 葛城之高額比売命 (reading unconfirmed), born when 多遅摩比多訶 married his niece 由良度美 (reading unconfirmed), was the mother of 息長帯比売命 (reading unconfirmed). The treasures Ame-no-Hiboko brought were called the jewel treasures (玉津宝): two strings of beads; the 振浪比礼, 切浪比礼, 振風比礼 and 切風比礼 scarves; and the 奥津鏡 and 辺津鏡 mirrors (reading unconfirmed), eight kinds in all; a note says that these are Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami (伊豆志之八前大神).

This deity had a daughter, Izushi-otome-no-Kami (伊豆志袁登売神). Many deities wished to marry her, but none could. The elder brother, Akiyama-no-Shitahi-otoko (秋山之下氷壮夫), asked his younger brother, Haruyama-no-Kasumi-otoko (春山之霞壮夫), "I sought her hand and failed. Can you win this maiden?" When the younger brother answered, "Easily," the elder brother said, "If you win her, I will take off my upper and lower garments and give them to you, brew sake in a jar as tall as my own height, and prepare everything from the mountains and rivers," and made a 宇礼豆玖 (reading unconfirmed) (wager). When the younger brother told his mother, his mother took 布遅葛 (reading unconfirmed) vine and in a single night wove and sewed a robe, trousers, socks and shoes, and also made a bow and arrows; she had the younger brother put them on and sent him to the maiden's house. Then the clothes and the bow and arrows all turned into wisteria flowers.

Haruyama-no-Kasumi-otoko (春山之霞壮夫) hung the bow and arrows at the maiden's privy, and Izushi-otome-no-Kami (伊豆志袁登売神), finding the flowers strange, was about to take them home. The younger brother followed behind her into the house and married her, and one child was born. But the elder brother, jealous of his younger brother's marriage, did not pay the stakes of the wager. Their mother, resentful of her elder son, had a coarse basket with eight meshes (八目荒籠) made from the bamboo of an island in the Izushi river (伊豆志河), mixed stones from the river with salt, wrapped them in bamboo leaves, had a curse laid saying, "As these bamboo leaves grow green and wither, so grow green and wither. As this salt ebbs and flows, so ebb and flow. As these stones sink, so sink and lie prostrate," and placed it above the smoke. Because of this the elder brother withered, sickened and wasted away for eight years; but when he wept and pleaded with his mother, she had the cursing objects returned, and the elder brother's body became well again as before. A note says this is the origin of the expression "神宇礼豆玖" (reading unconfirmed).

Also, 若野毛二俣王 (reading unconfirmed), son of Emperor 品陀 (reading unconfirmed), married his mother's younger sister 百師木伊呂弁 (reading unconfirmed) (also named 弟日売真若比売命), and seven children were born, including 大郎子 (also named 意富富杼王) and 忍坂之大中津比売命 (reading unconfirmed). 意富富杼王 is regarded as the ancestor of the 三国君, the 息長君 (reading unconfirmed) and others. Emperor 品陀 (Emperor Ōjin) died at the age of 130, and his tomb is at the 裳伏岡 of 恵賀 in 川内 (reading unconfirmed).

quotes.note: The light of the sun shone like a rainbow on the woman's private parts (what led to the birth of the red jewel).
When he placed the jewel beside his bed, it changed into a beautiful maiden.
The clothes and the bow and arrows that the mother made all turned into wisteria flowers.
As these bamboo leaves grow green and wither, so grow green and wither (part of the words of the curse the mother had laid on the elder brother).

figures.name: Akaru-hime-no-Kami (阿加流比賣神)
figures.role: The wife of Ame-no-Hiboko, born from a red jewel. Reviled by her husband, she fled to Naniwa and is regarded as the deity who dwells at the 比売碁曽社 shrine.

figures.name: Izushi-otome-no-Kami (伊豆志袁登賣神)
figures.role: A goddess recorded as "this deity's daughter" directly after Izushi-Yamae-no-Ōkami (伊豆志之八前大神). She married Haruyama-no-Kasumi-otoko.

figures.name: Akiyama-no-Shitahi-otoko (秋山之下氷壯夫)
figures.role: The elder brother deity. Though he lost the wager, he did not pay what he had promised, and suffered for eight years under his mother's curse.

figures.name: Haruyama-no-Kasumi-otoko (春山之霞壯夫)
figures.role: The younger brother deity. With his mother's help he married Izushi-otome-no-Kami and had a child.

figures.name: The mother (御祖)
figures.role: Mother of the autumn-mountain and spring-mountain brothers. She made wisteria clothes and a bow and arrows for the younger brother, had a curse laid on the elder brother who broke his promise, and later lifted it.

figures.name: 多遲麻毛理 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: A descendant of Ame-no-Hiboko four generations later, son of 多遅摩比那良岐.

figures.name: 葛城之高額比賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of 多遅摩比多訶 and 由良度美, and mother of 息長帯比売命.

figures.name: The jewel treasures (玉津寶)
figures.role: The eight treasures Ame-no-Hiboko brought (two strings of beads, the 振浪比礼, 切浪比礼, 振風比礼 and 切風比礼 scarves, and the 奥津鏡 and 辺津鏡 mirrors).

figures.name: 若野毛二俣王 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Son of Emperor 品陀. He married 百師木伊呂弁 and had seven children, including 意富富杼王.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 6 — the 3rd year of Emperor Suinin, spring, 3rd month
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, Ame-no-Hiboko (天日槍) is said to have come in the 3rd year of Emperor Suinin, and the treasures he brought were seven kinds, which were deposited in Tajima Province as the property of the deity. An alternative account (一云) in a small-script note says that he first arrived in Harima and came after yielding his land to his younger brother on hearing that there was a sage ruler (聖皇) in Japan, and gives the treasures as eight kinds. It does not say, as the Kojiki does, that he came in pursuit of his wife.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 6 — "this year" (是歳) of the 2nd year of Emperor Suinin (alternative account (一云) in a small-script note)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, a story in which a white stone turns into a beautiful maiden, who leaves and becomes the deity of the 比売語曾社 (reading unconfirmed) shrine in Naniwa, appears in an alternative account (一云) in a small-script note, not as a story of Ame-no-Hiboko but as a story of 都怒我阿羅斯等 (reading unconfirmed), son of the king of the land of 意富加羅 (reading unconfirmed). Its plot resembles the Kojiki story of Akaru-hime-no-Kami (阿加流比売神), in which a red jewel becomes a maiden who dwells at the 比売碁曽社 shrine in Naniwa.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 6 — the 88th year of Emperor Suinin, autumn, 7th month (己酉朔戊午)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the emperor says he wishes to see the divine treasures of Tajima and has 清彦 (reading unconfirmed), great-grandson of Ame-no-Hiboko, present them. Only the small sword of 出石 (reading unconfirmed) vanished and appeared on Awaji Island, where the islanders enshrined it. This story of the presentation is not in the Kojiki, and in the Kojiki 清日子 (reading unconfirmed) is a descendant of Ame-no-Hiboko four generations later.

nintoku-kamado.title: The Accession of Emperor Nintoku and the People's Hearths
