nintoku-kamado.lead: 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Nintoku) ruled the realm from the 高津宮 (reading unconfirmed) in Naniwa, and built one after another embankments and ponds, canals and ports. Seeing from a high mountain that no cooking smoke rose anywhere in the land, he exempted the people from labor levies and taxes (課役) for three years, and as the people grew prosperous, his reign was praised as "the reign of the sage emperor" (聖帝世).

points.text: 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Nintoku) looked over the land from a high mountain and, because no cooking smoke rose, knew that the whole land was poor, and exempted the people from all labor levies and taxes (課役) for three years. During that time, even when the palace fell into disrepair and rain leaked in, he had it left unrepaired and made do by catching the rain in vessels.

Seeing that smoke filled the land, the emperor imposed the labor levies and taxes again, but the common people (百姓) prospered and did not suffer from the labor. Therefore this reign was praised as "the reign of the sage emperor" (聖帝世).

In this reign, using the 秦人 (reading unconfirmed) people, the 茨田 embankment and the 三宅 of 茨田 (reading unconfirmed) were made, the 丸邇 Pond and the 依網 Pond (reading unconfirmed) were made, the 堀江 (reading unconfirmed) canal of Naniwa was dug to connect with the sea, the 小椅江 (reading unconfirmed) was dug, and the port of Suminoe (墨江津) was established.
Of the four sons born of the chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed), three, 伊邪本和気命, 水歯別命 and 男浅津間若子宿禰命 (reading unconfirmed), later ruled the realm.

In the Nihon Shoki (Book 11), he sees that no smoke rises from a "high tower" (高台); in the 2nd month of the 4th year he speaks of it to his ministers, and in the 3rd month he orders a three-year exemption from labor levies and taxes. In the 4th month of the 7th year, seeing that smoke filled the land, he has an exchange with the empress, and in the 10th month of the 10th year he imposes the labor levies and taxes and has the palace built, and the common people worked willingly day and night. The Kojiki gives no year or month.

The Kokugakuin University deity-name database introduces the view that the land of 墨江 (住吉, Sumiyoshi) was anciently called Suminoe, and that the role of the port (大津) serving as the royal power's base for external relations was carried by the port of Sumiyoshi (住吉津) until the first half of the sixth century, when it is said to have shifted to the port of Naniwa (難波津).

story.text: 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Nintoku) ruled the realm from the 高津宮 (reading unconfirmed) in Naniwa. He made 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 葛城之曾都毘古 (reading unconfirmed), his chief consort, and four sons were born: 大江之伊邪本和気命, 墨江之中津王, 蝮之水歯別命 and 男浅津間若子宿禰命 (reading unconfirmed). He also married 髪長比売 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 牛諸, the 諸県君 of Hyūga (reading unconfirmed), and 波多毘能大郎子 (also named 大日下王) and 波多毘能若郎女 (also named 長日比売命 and 若日下部命) (reading unconfirmed) were born.

The emperor also married his half-sisters 八田若郎女 and 宇遅能若郎女 (reading unconfirmed), but these two had no children. The text records that his children numbered six in all (five princes and one princess), and that three of them, 伊邪本和気命, 蝮之水歯別命 and 男浅津間若子宿禰命 (reading unconfirmed), later ruled the realm. As name-bearing groups (御名代), the 葛城部 was established for the chief consort, the 壬生部 for the crown prince 伊邪本和気命, the 蝮部 for 水歯別命, the 大日下部 for 大日下王, and the 若日下部 for 若日下部王 (reading unconfirmed).

In this reign, using the 秦人 (reading unconfirmed) people, the 茨田 embankment and the 三宅 of 茨田 (reading unconfirmed) were made, and the 丸邇 Pond and the 依網 Pond (reading unconfirmed) were made. Also, the 堀江 (reading unconfirmed) canal of Naniwa was dug to connect with the sea, the 小椅江 (reading unconfirmed) was dug, and the port of Suminoe (墨江津) was established.

Once the emperor climbed a high mountain, looked out over the lands in all four directions, and ordered, "No smoke is rising in the land. The whole land is poor. Therefore, from now on, for three years, exempt the people from all labor levies and taxes (課役)." Because of this the palace fell into disrepair and rain leaked in everywhere, but he did not have it repaired at all; he caught the leaking rain in vessels and moved to places where it did not leak.

Later, when he looked over the land, smoke filled the land. Judging that the people had become prosperous, the emperor imposed the labor levies and taxes again. Thus the common people (百姓) prospered and did not suffer from the labor. The text records that therefore that reign was praised and called "the reign of the sage emperor" (聖帝世).

quotes.note: No smoke is rising in the land. The whole land is poor (the emperor's words).
Exempt the people from all labor levies and taxes (課役).
He caught the leaking rain in vessels.
That reign is praised and called "the reign of the sage emperor" (聖帝世).

figures.name: 大雀命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Nintoku)
figures.role: Emperor Nintoku. He ruled the realm from the 高津宮 in Naniwa, exempted the people from labor levies and taxes for three years, and was praised as "the sage emperor" (聖帝).

figures.name: 石之日賣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of 葛城之曾都毘古 and chief consort. She bore four sons, and the 葛城部 was established as her name-bearing group (御名代).

figures.name: 葛城之曾都毘古 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Father of the chief consort 石之日売命.

figures.name: 髮長比賣 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: Daughter of 牛諸, the 諸県君 of Hyūga. She bore 大日下王 and 若日下部命.

figures.name: 伊邪本和氣命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The chief consort's eldest son and crown prince. He later ruled the realm. The 壬生部 was established as his name-bearing group (御名代).

figures.name: 蝮之水齒別命 (reading unconfirmed)

compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the emperor gazes far out from a high tower (高台), sees that no smoke rises, and issues an edict to his ministers lamenting the poverty of the common people. The way the place is described differs from the Kojiki's "climbed a high mountain," and the year and month are recorded.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 11 — the 7th year of Emperor Nintoku, summer, 4th month (辛未朔)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, there is an exchange in which the emperor, seeing that smoke filled the land, says to the empress, "We are already rich," and, when the empress asks how this can be when even the palace fence is in ruins, answers that when the common people are rich, the emperor too is rich. The Kojiki does not have this exchange.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 11 — the 10th year of Emperor Nintoku, winter, 10th month
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, even after receiving the requests of the provinces he still waits, and only in the 10th month of the 10th year does he impose labor levies and taxes and have the palace built; the common people, bringing the old and the young, carried the timber themselves, and it was soon completed, and that is why he is still called "the sage emperor" (聖帝) today.

nintoku-kurohime.title: The Jealousy of 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) and 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed)
nintoku-kurohime.lead: Fearing the jealousy of the chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed), 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed), who had been summoned from Kibi, fled back to her home, and the chief consort had her put off the boat and made her walk home. The emperor, falsely saying he was going to view 淡道嶋 (reading unconfirmed), went all the way to Kibi to visit 黒日売, and the two exchanged songs.

points.text: The chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was extremely jealous, and 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of the 海部直 (reading unconfirmed) of Kibi, who had been summoned by the emperor, fled back to her home in fear of the chief consort. Still angry, the chief consort had 黒日売 driven off the boat at 大浦 (reading unconfirmed) and made her walk home.

The emperor deceived the chief consort, saying, "I wish to view 淡道嶋" (reading unconfirmed), and set out; after gazing far out from 淡道嶋 and singing, he went from island to island to the province of Kibi and met 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed).

In Kibi, 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed) welcomed the emperor at a place in the 山方 (reading unconfirmed) and offered him the imperial meal, and the emperor sang at the place where the 菘菜 (reading unconfirmed) greens were being picked. When the emperor returned, 黒日売 presented two songs.

According to the Kokugakuin University deity-name database, the song the emperor sang on 淡道嶋 (reading unconfirmed) is thought to be a land-viewing (国見) song set against the background of the myth of the birth of the islands, and there is a theory that Onogoroshima (淤能碁呂島) and Awashima (淡島) were included in it as mythical islands representing the land ruled by the royal power. There is also a theory that takes "佐気都志摩" (reading unconfirmed) ("detached island") in the song to be 吉備児島 (reading unconfirmed), showing the bond between the royal power and Kibi.

The entry for 須勢理毘売 (reading unconfirmed) in the same database cites the story of 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) as a tradition of a principal wife who is jealous of other wives, and introduces a theory that sees it not as a mere love story but as telling of a struggle for leadership of rituals among women who, like shrine maidens (巫女), were in charge of worship.

The story of 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed) could not be confirmed in Book 11 (Emperor Nintoku) of the Nihon Shoki. However, in an entry for the 7th month of the 16th year, the emperor says that because of the empress's jealousy he has been unable to be united with the palace lady 桑田玖賀媛 (reading unconfirmed), and gives her to 速待 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the governors of Harima (播磨国造).

story.text: The chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was extremely jealous, and the concubines the emperor kept in his service could not even peep into the palace. The text records that whenever there was anything to be said, the chief consort was so jealous that she stamped her feet.

The emperor heard of 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of the 海部直 (reading unconfirmed) of Kibi, who was beautiful in appearance, summoned her, and kept her in his service. But 黒日売, fearing the chief consort's jealousy, fled down to her home province. The emperor, from a high terrace, watched 黒日売's boat floating out onto the sea, and sang a song.

Hearing this song, the chief consort was furious; she sent people to 大浦 (reading unconfirmed) to drive 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed) off the boat and made her walk home. The emperor, longing for 黒日売, deceived the chief consort, saying, "I wish to view 淡道嶋" (reading unconfirmed), and set out. On reaching 淡道嶋, he gazed far out and sang a song. That song includes the names of islands such as Awashima (阿波志摩, 淡島) and Onogoroshima (淤能碁呂志摩).

From that island the emperor went from island to island to the province of Kibi. 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed) welcomed the emperor at a place in the 山方 (reading unconfirmed) of that province and offered him the imperial meal. When 黒日売 was picking the 菘菜 (reading unconfirmed) greens of that land to cook the imperial soup (大御羹), the emperor came to the place where she was picking and sang a song.
When the emperor returned to the capital, 黒日売 (reading unconfirmed) presented a song, and then sang one more. Both songs begin with the words "夜麻登幣邇" (reading unconfirmed) ("toward Yamato").

nintoku-yamashiro.title: The Chief Consort's Journey to 山代 (reading unconfirmed) and the Six Songs
nintoku-yamashiro.lead: While the chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was away in 木国 (reading unconfirmed) to gather 御綱柏 (reading unconfirmed) leaves, the emperor married 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed). When the chief consort learned of it, she threw the 御綱柏 into the sea and, without returning to the palace, headed for 山代 (reading unconfirmed); the emperor sent messengers and songs, and in the end went himself to the house of 奴理能美 (reading unconfirmed) at 筒木 (reading unconfirmed) and sang.

points.text: While the chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was away in 木国 (reading unconfirmed) to gather 御綱柏 (reading unconfirmed) leaves, the emperor married 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed). Learning of it from a laborer's (仕丁) talk on the boat home, the chief consort threw all the 御綱柏 into the sea (the origin of the name 御津前 (reading unconfirmed) for that place), and without entering the palace went up the 堀江 canal toward 山代 (reading unconfirmed).

The emperor's messenger, 丸邇臣口子 (reading unconfirmed), in heavy rain, lay prostrate in the courtyard immersed in water up to his waist, and his blue-printed robe (青摺衣) was dyed red by the color of its crimson cords. His younger sister 口日売 (reading unconfirmed), who served the chief consort, saw this and sang a song.

The three, 口子臣, 口比売 and 奴理能美 (reading unconfirmed), had it reported to the emperor that the chief consort had only come to see a wondrous insect that changes into three forms. Saying that he would see the insect, the emperor visited 奴理能美's house and sang at the door of the chief consort's hall. The six songs of the two are regarded as the "志都歌之歌返" (reading unconfirmed).

In the Nihon Shoki, the empress goes to the cape of Kumano (熊野岬) in Kii (紀国), and the place where she threw the leaves into the sea is named "葉済" (reading unconfirmed). The empress built a palace south of the 筒城岡 (reading unconfirmed) hill in 山背 (reading unconfirmed) and lived there; even when the emperor went to the 筒城宮 (reading unconfirmed) palace she would not meet him, and she did not return, giving as her reason that he had made 八田皇女 (reading unconfirmed) his consort. The story of the wondrous insect does not appear, and the empress dies at the 筒城宮 palace in the 35th year.
The Kokugakuin University deity-name database interprets "伊斯祁" (ishike), in the song the emperor entrusted to 鳥山 (reading unconfirmed), as shiku, meaning "to reach, to catch up."
The same database interprets "夜賀波延那須" (yagahaenasu), in the song the emperor sang at the door, as a simile for a figure leading a great number of retainers.

story.text: After that, the chief consort went to 木国 (reading unconfirmed) to gather 御綱柏 (reading unconfirmed) leaves for a banquet (豊楽). Meanwhile the emperor married 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed). While the chief consort was on her way home with her boat fully loaded with 御綱柏, a laborer (仕丁) from 児嶋 in the province of Kibi (reading unconfirmed), who had been employed in the Water Office (水取司) and was on his way home to his province, met at the great crossing (大渡) of Naniwa the boat of a storehouse woman (倉人女) who was following behind, and said, "The emperor has recently married 八田若郎女 and amuses himself with her day and night. The chief consort has not heard of this, which is surely why she is traveling at her leisure." The storehouse woman at once caught up with the chief consort's boat and reported it to her just as she had heard it.

The chief consort, deeply resentful and angry, threw all the 御綱柏 (reading unconfirmed) loaded on her boat into the sea. Therefore that place is called 御津前 (reading unconfirmed). Without entering the palace, the chief consort had her boat hauled up the 堀江 (reading unconfirmed) canal, went up along the river to 山代 (reading unconfirmed), and sang a song. Then, going round from 山代, she reached the entrance of 那良山 (reading unconfirmed) and sang another song.

The chief consort turned back and for a while stayed at the house of 奴理能美 (reading unconfirmed), a 韓人 of 筒木 (reading unconfirmed). Hearing that the chief consort had gone up by way of 山代, the emperor sent his attendant (舎人) 鳥山 (reading unconfirmed) with a song. He then sent 丸邇臣口子 (reading unconfirmed) with two songs.

When 口子臣 (reading unconfirmed) came to deliver these songs, heavy rain was falling. 口子臣, not avoiding the rain, lay prostrate at the front door of the hall, but the chief consort went out by the back door; when he lay prostrate at the back door, she went out by the front door. 口子臣 crawled forward and knelt in the middle of the courtyard, and the pooled water reached his waist. Because he was wearing a blue-printed robe (青摺衣) with crimson cords, the water touched the crimson cords and the blue robe turned completely red. 口子臣's younger sister 口日売 (reading unconfirmed), who served the chief consort, saw this and sang a song.

When the chief consort asked the reason, 口日売 (reading unconfirmed) answered, "It is my elder brother, 口子臣." So the three, 口子臣, 口比売 and 奴理能美 (reading unconfirmed), consulted together and had it reported to the emperor: "The reason the chief consort has come is only to see the insect that 奴理能美 keeps, which becomes a crawling insect, then a shell, then a flying bird, a wondrous insect that changes into three forms; she has no other intention." The emperor said, "Then I too wish to see it," and went up from the great palace and entered 奴理能美's house. 奴理能美 presented the insect that changes into three kinds to the chief consort, and the emperor stood at the door of the hall where the chief consort was and sang a song.

The text records that these six songs sung by the emperor and the chief consort are the "志都歌之歌返" (reading unconfirmed). Next, the emperor, longing for 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed), sent her a song (continued in the next story).

When (口子臣 (reading unconfirmed)) knelt in the middle of the courtyard, the pooled water reached his waist.

medori.title: 八田若郎女, 女鳥王 and 速総別王 (readings unconfirmed)
medori.lead: Using his younger brother 速総別王 (reading unconfirmed) as a go-between, the emperor sought 女鳥王 (reading unconfirmed), but she refused, giving the strength of the chief consort as her reason, and became the wife of 速総別王. On hearing a song by 女鳥王, the emperor raised an army, and the two were killed at 蘇邇 (reading unconfirmed) in Uda. The general 山部大楯連 (reading unconfirmed), who had taken 女鳥王’s jewelled bracelet, was also put to death by the chief consort.

points.text: Using his younger brother 速総別王 (reading unconfirmed) as a go-between, the emperor sought 女鳥王 (reading unconfirmed), but she refused, saying, “Because the chief consort is so strong, the emperor has not even taken 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed) as his wife,” and she became the wife of 速総別王. 速総別王 gave the emperor no reply.

When the emperor visited 女鳥王, she was weaving at her loom. Learning her feelings through an exchange of songs, the emperor went back for the time being, but when he heard the song 女鳥王 sang when 速総別王 came to her, he immediately raised an army.
速総別王 and 女鳥王 climbed Mount 倉椅山 (reading unconfirmed) and fled further, but the emperor’s army caught up with them at 蘇邇 (reading unconfirmed) in Uda, and they were killed.

The general 山部大楯連 (reading unconfirmed) took the jewelled bracelet (玉釧) from 女鳥王’s arm and gave it to his wife. At a banquet (豊楽), the chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) noticed it, and she had 大楯連 put to death for the crime of stripping his lord’s bracelet from her while her skin was still warm.
The emperor and 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed) exchanged songs, and the 八田部 (reading unconfirmed) was established as a namesake group (御名代) for 八田若郎女.

In the Nihon Shoki, this story is placed in the 2nd month of the 40th year of Emperor Nintoku, and the names are written 雌鳥皇女 and 隼別皇子 (readings unconfirmed). The two were killed at 蒋代野 (reading unconfirmed) in Ise while trying to reach the Ise Shrine. The person who took the jewel was the pursuer 佐伯直阿俄能胡 (reading unconfirmed), who escaped the death penalty by offering up his own land (that land is called 玉代). In the Nihon Shoki, the empress at this time is 八田皇女 (reading unconfirmed), who had been made empress in the 38th year.

story.text: The emperor sent a song to 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed), and 八田若郎女 also answered with a song. He then established the 八田部 (reading unconfirmed) as a namesake group (御名代) for 八田若郎女.

The emperor also used his younger brother 速総別王 (reading unconfirmed) as a go-between to seek his half-sister 女鳥王 (reading unconfirmed) as a wife. But 女鳥王 told 速総別王, “Because the chief consort is so strong, the emperor has not even properly taken 八田若郎女 as his wife. So I do not intend to serve him. I will be your wife,” and the two were married. For this reason 速総別王 gave the emperor no reply.

The emperor went in person to where 女鳥王 lived and sat on the threshold of the palace door. 女鳥王 was at her loom, weaving cloth. When the emperor sang a song, 女鳥王 answered with a song, and in her song the name 速総別 (波夜夫佐和気) was sung. Knowing her feelings, the emperor returned to his palace.

Later, when her husband 速総別王 came, 女鳥王 sang a song. When the emperor heard this song, he immediately raised an army to kill the two. 速総別王 and 女鳥王 fled together and climbed Mount 倉椅山 (reading unconfirmed), and 速総別王 sang two songs. The two fled further from there, but when they reached 蘇邇 (reading unconfirmed) in Uda, the emperor’s army caught up with them and killed them.

The general at that time, 山部大楯連 (reading unconfirmed), took the jewelled bracelet (玉釧) that 女鳥王 wore on her arm and gave it to his own wife. Later a banquet (豊楽) was held, and when the women of all the clans came to the palace, 大楯連’s wife came wearing that bracelet on her arm. The chief consort 石之日売命 (reading unconfirmed) was herself taking the oak leaves (柏) of great sake and handing them to the women, but when she noticed the bracelet, she did not give a leaf to the wife and sent her away. The chief consort summoned 大楯連 and said, “Those royals were set aside because they were disrespectful, and that was only right. But you, a mere retainer, stripped the bracelet from your lord’s arm while her skin was still warm and gave it to your own wife.” She then had him put to death.

quotes.note: Because the chief consort is strong, (the emperor) has not even taken 八田若郎女 (reading unconfirmed) as his wife (the words of 女鳥王).
When the emperor heard this song, he immediately raised an army to kill them.
When they reached 蘇邇 (reading unconfirmed) in Uda, the emperor’s army caught up with them and killed them.
You stripped off the bracelet worn on your lord’s arm while her skin was still warm and brought it away (the words of the chief consort).

compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, 隼別皇子 (reading unconfirmed), resting his head on the lap of 雌鳥皇女 (reading unconfirmed), asked, “Which is faster, the wren (鷦鷯) or the falcon (隼)?”, and on hearing “The falcon is faster,” said, “So I come first,” and this deepened the emperor’s resentment. This exchange is not in the Kojiki.

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 11, the 40th year of Emperor Nintoku, this year
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, it is the empress who, at the 新嘗 harvest banquet, notices a jewel resembling the princess’s, and the person who took the jewel is 佐伯直阿俄能胡 (reading unconfirmed). 阿俄能胡 was pardoned from the death penalty by offering up his own land, and that land was called “玉代”. In the Kojiki, 山部大楯連 (reading unconfirmed) is put to death.

nintoku-kari.title: The Song of the Wild Goose’s Eggs and the Ship 枯野 (reading unconfirmed)
nintoku-kari.lead: The emperor asked Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto in a song about a wild goose laying eggs on 日女嶋 (reading unconfirmed), and Takeuchi-no-Sukune answered in a song. In this reign a fast ship, “枯野” (reading unconfirmed), was made from a huge tree, and from the ship’s charred remains a koto (zither) was made whose sound carried for seven ri.

points.text: In a song, the emperor asked Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto (建内宿禰) about a wild goose having laid eggs on 日女嶋 (reading unconfirmed), and Takeuchi-no-Sukune answered in a song. The song he then sang after being granted the emperor’s koto is described as “the 片歌 of the 本岐歌” (readings unconfirmed).

The tall tree west of the 免寸河 river (reading unconfirmed) was so large that its shadow in the morning sun reached Awaji Island (淡道嶋) and its shadow in the evening sun crossed Mount 高安山 (reading unconfirmed). The fast ship made from this tree was “枯野” (reading unconfirmed), and morning and evening it carried cold spring water from Awaji Island as drinking water for the emperor (大御水).

When 枯野 (reading unconfirmed) broke down, it was used as fuel for making salt, and a koto made from its charred remains had a sound that carried for seven ri. The song sung then is described as “the 歌返 of the 志都歌” (readings unconfirmed).
It is recorded that Emperor Nintoku lived to the age of eighty-three and that his tomb is at 耳原 in Mozu (毛受之耳原; reading unconfirmed).

In the Nihon Shoki, the wild goose laid its eggs in the 3rd month of the 50th year, at the 茨田堤 embankment (reading unconfirmed) in Kawachi, and the emperor asks Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto (武内宿禰) in a song after sending a messenger to confirm it. There is no scene in which he is granted the koto and sings a 片歌. The story of the ship 枯野 and the koto could not be confirmed in Book 11; instead there is an entry for the 62nd year in which a ship is ordered to be built from a great tree in Tōtōmi.

Kokugakuin University’s database of deity names, touching on the view that Takamimusubi-no-Kami (高御産巣日神, also called 高木神) was originally a sun deity, notes that a connection between huge trees and the sun can be seen in the huge-tree legend of the “枯野 ship” in the section on Emperor Nintoku.

story.text: Once, the emperor went to 日女嶋 (reading unconfirmed) intending to hold a banquet (豊楽). On that island a wild goose laid eggs. The emperor therefore summoned Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto (建内宿禰命) and asked him in a song about the wild goose laying eggs.
Takeuchi-no-Sukune answered in a song, and then, having been granted the emperor’s koto, sang a song. The text records that this song is “the 片歌 of the 本岐歌” (readings unconfirmed).

In this reign there was a single tall tree west of the 免寸河 river (reading unconfirmed). When the morning sun struck it, its shadow reached as far as Awaji Island (淡道嶋), and when the evening sun struck it, its shadow crossed Mount 高安山 (reading unconfirmed). So this tree was cut down and made into a ship, and it became a ship that sailed very fast. The ship was named “枯野” (reading unconfirmed), and with it, morning and evening, cold spring water from Awaji Island was drawn and offered as drinking water for the emperor (大御水).

When this ship broke down, it was burned to make salt, and a koto was made from the wood left unburned. Its sound carried as far as seven ri. A song was sung about this, and the text records that this song is “the 歌返 of the 志都歌” (readings unconfirmed).
The emperor lived to the age of eighty-three, and his tomb is at 耳原 in Mozu (毛受之耳原; reading unconfirmed).

quotes.note: On that island a wild goose laid eggs.
When the morning sun struck it, the tree’s shadow reached Awaji Island (淡道嶋), and when the evening sun struck it, the shadow crossed Mount 高安山 (reading unconfirmed).
The ship was named “枯野” (reading unconfirmed).
When a koto was made, its sound carried for seven ri.

figures.name: 枯野 (reading unconfirmed)

compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, a person from Kawachi reports that a wild goose has laid eggs at the 茨田堤 embankment (reading unconfirmed), and after sending a messenger to confirm it, the emperor asks Takeuchi-no-Sukune-no-Mikoto (武内宿禰) in a song. The place differs from the Kojiki’s 日女嶋 (reading unconfirmed), and there is no 片歌 sung by Takeuchi-no-Sukune after being granted the koto.

Instead, there is an entry in which 倭直吾子篭 (reading unconfirmed) is ordered to build a ship from a great tree that had drifted down the 大井河 river (reading unconfirmed) in Tōtōmi Province, and to bring it to the port of Naniwa (難波津).

compare.where: Nihon Shoki, Book 11, the 87th year of Emperor Nintoku, winter, 10th month (癸未朔己丑)
compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the emperor dies in the 1st month of the 87th year and is buried in the 10th month of the same year in the 百舌鳥野 tomb (reading unconfirmed); his age is not recorded. The Kojiki gives his age as eighty-three and places his tomb at 毛受之耳原 (reading unconfirmed).

richu.title: Emperor Richū, Emperor Hanzei and the Revolt of 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed)
richu.lead: While 伊邪本和気命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Richū) lay asleep drunk, his younger brother 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed) set fire to his great hall; rescued by 阿知直 (reading unconfirmed), he escaped to Isonokami Shrine (石上神宮). His younger brother 水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed), ordered to clear himself of suspicion, had the Hayato 曾婆訶理 (reading unconfirmed) kill 墨江中王 and then cut down that Hayato as well; later 水歯別命 ruled the realm as Emperor Hanzei.

points.text: At the banquet (豊明) of the Great Thanksgiving (大嘗) at the Naniwa palace (難波宮), while 伊邪本和気命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Richū) lay asleep drunk on sake, his younger brother 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed) set fire to the great hall, intending to kill the emperor. 阿知直 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 倭漢直 (reading unconfirmed), put the emperor on a horse and sent him away to Yamato (倭).

At the entrance to Mount 大坂山 (reading unconfirmed), told by a woman, the emperor went round by the 当岐麻道 road (reading unconfirmed) and entered Isonokami Shrine (石上神宮). He suspected his younger brother 水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed), who came there, and ordered him to kill 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed) before coming to him.

水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed) promised the Hayato 曾婆訶理 (reading unconfirmed) the rank of minister and had him kill 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed) in the privy; but holding that killing one’s own lord was unrighteous, at the banquet where he conferred the rank of minister, he cut off 曾婆訶理’s head. The place he went up to the next day was named Near Asuka (近飛鳥), and the place where he stayed to perform purification (祓禊) was named Far Asuka (遠飛鳥).

Emperor Richū lived to the age of sixty-four, and his tomb is at Mozu (毛受). The following ruler, 水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Hanzei), governed from the 柴垣宮 palace at 多治比 (readings unconfirmed). It is recorded that he was nine shaku two and a half sun tall and that his teeth, upper and lower, were even, like strung beads. He lived to the age of sixty, and his tomb is in the plain of Mozu (毛受野).

In the Nihon Shoki, the incident begins when 住吉仲皇子 (reading unconfirmed) goes to 黒媛 (reading unconfirmed) using the crown prince’s name, and the crown prince is rescued by three men: 平群木菟宿禰, 物部大前宿禰 and 阿知使主 (readings unconfirmed). The one who stabs 仲皇子 is his attendant, the Hayato 刺領巾 (reading unconfirmed), and 木菟宿禰 advises that a man who has killed his own lord cannot be allowed to live, whereupon 刺領巾 is killed.

Kokugakuin University’s database of deity names explains that Isonokami Shrine (石上神宮) served as a divine storehouse and armoury holding the sacred treasures of the royal power, and that, together with Ise and Izumo, it was one of the few shrines called a “jingū” (神宮) in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki.

story.text: 伊邪本和気命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Richū) ruled the realm from the 若桜宮 palace at 伊波礼 (readings unconfirmed). He married 黒比売命 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 葦田宿禰 (reading unconfirmed), son of 葛城之曾都毘古 (reading unconfirmed), and 市辺之忍歯王, 御馬王 and 青海郎女 (also called 飯豊郎女) (readings unconfirmed) were born.

When the emperor was still at the Naniwa palace (難波宮), at the banquet (豊明) after the Great Thanksgiving (大嘗), he became drunk on sake and fell asleep. At that time his younger brother 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed) set fire to the great hall, intending to kill the emperor. 阿知直 (reading unconfirmed), ancestor of the 倭漢直 (reading unconfirmed), carried the emperor out, put him on a horse and sent him toward Yamato (倭). When the emperor awoke at 多遅比野 (reading unconfirmed) and asked, “Where is this?”, 阿知直 answered that 墨江中王 had set fire to the great hall, so he was taking him and fleeing to Yamato. The emperor sang a song, and when he reached the 波邇賦坂 slope (reading unconfirmed) and looked back toward the Naniwa palace, the fire was still burning, so he sang again.

At the entrance to Mount 大坂山 (reading unconfirmed) he met a woman. She told him, “Many armed men are blocking this mountain. Go round by the 当岐麻道 road (reading unconfirmed) and cross that way,” and the emperor sang a song. In this way the emperor went up and entered Isonokami Shrine (石上神宮).

His younger brother by the same mother, 水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed), came to him, but the emperor sent word: “I suspect that you are of the same mind as 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed), so I will not meet and speak with you.” When 水歯別命 replied, “I have no impure heart, and I am not of one mind with 墨江中王,” the emperor ordered, “Then go back to Naniwa and kill 墨江中王 and come. Then I will certainly meet and speak with you.” 水歯別命 returned to Naniwa and approached 曾婆訶理 (reading unconfirmed), a Hayato who served close to 墨江中王, saying, “If you do as I say, I will become emperor, make you a minister, and rule the realm,” and he gave him many goods. 曾婆訶理 watched for his master to enter the privy and stabbed him to death with a spear.

On the way up to Yamato with 曾婆訶理 (reading unconfirmed), 水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed) reflected at the entrance to Mount 大坂山 (reading unconfirmed): “曾婆訶理 has done me a great service, but killing his own lord is unrighteous. Yet if I do not reward his service, I will be faithless. Even as I keep my promise, his heart is fearsome. So I will reward his service, but destroy him.” He therefore built a temporary palace, held a banquet (豊楽), conferred the rank of minister on the Hayato, and had the officials bow to him. It came about that he would drink sake from the same cup as the delighted Hayato; sake was poured into a bowl so large it hid the face, and the prince drank first and the Hayato after. As the Hayato drank, the great bowl covered his face, and the prince took out the sword he had placed beneath his seat and cut off his head.

Because he went up the next day, that place is called Near Asuka (近飛鳥). On reaching Yamato he said, “Today I will stay here and perform purification (祓禊), and tomorrow I will go up and worship at the shrine,” so that place is called Far Asuka (遠飛鳥). He then went to Isonokami Shrine (石上神宮) and sent word that “the matter has already been settled,” and the emperor called him in and spoke with him. The emperor appointed 阿知直 (reading unconfirmed) for the first time as an official of the storehouses (蔵官) and granted him land for provisions (粮地). In this reign he also granted the names or titles 若桜部 and 比売陀君 (readings unconfirmed) and established the 伊波礼部 (reading unconfirmed). The emperor lived to the age of sixty-four, and his tomb is at Mozu (毛受).

水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed; Emperor Hanzei) ruled the realm from the 柴垣宮 palace at 多治比 (readings unconfirmed). The emperor was nine shaku two and a half sun tall, and his teeth were one sun long and two bu wide, even above and below, like strung beads. He married 都怒郎女 (reading unconfirmed), daughter of 許碁登臣 of 丸邇 (readings unconfirmed), and 甲斐郎女 and 都夫良郎女 (readings unconfirmed) were born; he married 弟比売 (reading unconfirmed), another daughter of the same 臣, and 財王 and 多訶弁郎女 (readings unconfirmed) were born. His children numbered four in all. He lived to the age of sixty, and his tomb is in the plain of Mozu (毛受野).

quotes.note: Merry with sake, he fell asleep.
(墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed)) set fire to the great hall.
He has done me a great service, but he killed his own lord. This is unrighteous (the thoughts of 水歯別命 (reading unconfirmed)).
(Emperor Hanzei’s) teeth were one sun long and two bu wide, even above and below, like strung beads.

figures.name: 伊邪本和氣命 (reading unconfirmed)

figures.name: 水齒別命 (reading unconfirmed)
figures.role: The emperor’s younger brother by the same mother. He cleared himself of suspicion by bringing down 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed), and later ruled as Emperor Hanzei.

compare.text: In the Nihon Shoki, the messenger 住吉仲皇子 (reading unconfirmed), using the crown prince’s (Richū’s) name, visits 黒媛 (reading unconfirmed), whom the crown prince intended to make his consort, and fearing that this would become known, 仲皇子 raises troops and burns the crown prince’s palace. The Kojiki records only that 墨江中王 (reading unconfirmed) set the fire and gives no reason.

There is no story, as with the Kojiki’s 曾婆訶理, of a banquet held to confer the rank of minister at which he is cut down.
